#### 4.7 Simulating Weibull Random Variables

As we discussed in Chapter 1, random variables may be simulated through the use of the uniform random variable defined in the interval (0,1) and inverse expressions for the desired CDFs. Specifically, if F is any CDF with an inverse  $F^{-1}$ , then by substituting the unit uniform random variable U for p in the inverse expression  $F^{-1}(p)$ , we generate a random variable distributed according to F.

For the Weibull distribution with shape parameter  $\beta$  and characteristic life  $\alpha$ , the inverse expression is as follows:

$$F^{-1}(p) = t = \alpha - \ln(1 - F(t))^{1/\beta}$$

Thus, substitution of the unit uniform random variable U for p = F(t) gives the following:

$$F^{-1}(U) = t = \alpha [-\ln(1-U)]^{1/\beta}$$

Because 1 - U and U both represent a uniformly distributed variate in the interval (0,1), for purposes of simulation, we may write the inverse expression as follows:

$$F^{-1}(U) = t = \alpha [-\ln U]^{1/\beta}$$

To generate samples from U (i.e., from a uniformly distributed variate defined on the unit interval), we can use the spreadsheet function RAND(). We can also use the JMP

formula editor to generate uniformly distributed variables. More directly, we can use Minitab (open **Calc** to **Random Data** to **Weibull**) to simulate Weibull data with our choice of characteristic life (scale) and shape parameter.

NOTE: JMP 7 or later has the capability to directly simulate Weibull data.

#### Class Project 4.1: Simulating Weibull Random Variables

A method to generate the unit uniform random variables is needed. Calculators with such a capability may be used. The spreadsheet function RAND() is an easy approach. However, if a supply of 10-sided dice of various colors is obtainable, rolling the dice can be fun and instructive. Each student takes three different colored 10-sided dice and designates one color as the first digit, the second color as the second digit, and the third color as the last digit. Thus, the roll of the three dice will simulate a uniform random variable in the interval 0 to 999. Adding 1 to the number so obtained and dividing by 1000 will make the interval 0.001 to 1.000.

Each student rolls the three dice 10 times to simulate 10 uniform pseudorandom variables. Add 1 to each number and divide by 1000 to get 10 uniform unit random variables in the interval (0.001, 1.000). Substitute each value for U so obtained into the Weibull inverse expression. One-third of the class will use the shape parameter  $\beta$  = 0.5; one-third,  $\beta$  = 2; the remaining one-third will use  $\beta$  = 10. The characteristic life  $\alpha$  will be equal to 100 hours in all cases.

As a result, each student generates 10 pseudorandom, unordered, Weibull variables based on specific parameters. Those students with the same  $\beta$  value will combine results and draw a histogram on the blackboard or on an overhead transparency for other class members to view. Each student may wish to calculate the median time to failure and compare with the median expected from the formula:

$$\alpha(\ln 2)^{1/\beta} = \alpha(0.6931)^{1/\beta}$$

#### 4.8 The Three-Parameter Weibull Distribution

As described in Section 3.14 for the exponential, we can add a location parameter to the Weibull model by introducing a waiting or threshold time before which failures cannot occur. The three-parameter Weibull density function is

$$f(t) = \frac{\beta}{t - \alpha} \frac{t - \alpha}{\alpha} e^{-((t - \alpha)/\alpha)\beta}, \leq t < \infty$$

$$= 0 \quad \text{for} \quad t < \infty$$

*Weibull Distribution* 113

One example where a threshold parameter might make sense is the following scenario: A population of components has a wear-out failure mechanism based on the time it takes for the first of many competing dendritic metallic growths to cross a gap and cause a short. A Weibull model is a reasonable choice for this extreme value type failure mode. However, it is known that a certain level of moisture is needed within the encapsulated component before the dendrite growth process can start. The components begin life with little or no moisture present, and it takes time for water vapor to pass through the capsule cover and build up around the circuitry. The amount of waiting time, before which no failures can begin to occur, would be the parameter μ.

When you analyze data from a three-parameter Weibull population where μ is known from physical theory or other experimental data, subtract that known value from all data times and analyze the resulting data using the methods we have discussed for the twoparameter Weibull. If μ is unknown, the MLE ˆ is the smallest observed failure time in the sample data. Subtract this ˆ from all data times and you can again analyze the resulting data using the methods we have discussed for the two-parameter Weibull. For further discussion of this topic, see Lawless (2003).

#### **4.9 Goodness of Fit for the Weibull**

The chi-square goodness-of-fit test (Section 3.8), or the more powerful empirical distribution function (EDF)-based tests (Section 3.9), will test for Weibull goodness of fit, using the Weibull CDF expression and Weibull MLEs.

#### **4.10 Summary**

The Weibull distribution, with CDF *F t <sup>t</sup>* ( ) e / = − −( ) 1 <sup>α</sup> <sup>β</sup> , is a flexible, convenient life distribution model. It has a family of polynomial shaped failure rate functions, depending on the value of the shape parameter β, including decreasing, constant, and increasing failure rates. Many components and systems have reliability properties that are successfully modeled by the Weibull.

The Weibull also has a theoretical derivation as an extreme value distribution applying to the smallest random time of failure out of many independent competing failure processes. Consequently, one expects the Weibull will apply when failure occurs at a defect site within a material, and there are many such sites competing with each other to be the first to produce a failure. Capacitor dielectric material is an example, and the Weibull distribution has proved very successful as a model for capacitor lifetime.

The best way to analyze Weibull data and to estimate β and α is by the technique of MLE. For censored data, readout data, or truncated data, special computer programs are needed. However, these programs are readily available today, and the examples using JMP, Minitab, and Excel are shown in this chapter. A less optimal estimation procedure uses least squares and is equivalent to fitting a line to the data on Weibull graph paper, using an objective regression procedure. Whatever method is used for the final parameter estimates, Weibull data plots, as shown in Chapter 6, should be part of the analysis.

#### **4.3A Spreadsheet Likelihood Profile Confidence Intervals for Weibull Parameters**

The theoretical basis for likelihood profile confidence intervals is described in Chapter 8 (Sections 8.4 and 8.5). Here, we show how to use the Genweibest.xls spreadsheet, starting after convergence to MLEs as shown in Figure 4.3A, to find (two-sided) confidence intervals for the parameters α and β. First, choose the (two-sided) confidence level, or 100 × (1 – *p*)%, and pick the corresponding number from Table 4.1A.

These adjustment constants are just chi-square (with one degree of freedom) percentiles, divided by 2. They can be calculated with the spreadsheet expression = CHIINV(*p*, 1)/2.

We add the appropriate constant to the minimized *L* value shown in Figure 4.3A to obtain a new *L* target value. For a 95% confidence interval, the new *L* target is 91.41390 + 1.92073 = 93.33463.

The method requires four separate iterative searches, two for the upper and lower bound of β, and two more for the upper and lower bound of α. While this method sounds onerous, after a little practice, the iterations go quite rapidly and are usually quick to converge to the MLE final values. We will show the calculations for β bounds in detail and leave the bounds for α as an exercise.

Each iteration involves using the spreadsheet function **Goal Seek**, followed by a use of **Solver**. Both are found in the **Tools** menu.

The value in B2, after the second iteration, is 0.9066. One more iteration, not shown, brings us to the start of the fourth iteration, as shown in Figure 4.9A. When **Goal Seek** is run (for the fourth time), there is no change in B2 or H2, indicating that convergence has already occurred. The upper limit for β is 0.9069. This agrees with the limit given by JMP in Figure 4.9 (the reciprocal of 1.10266 = the lower bound for **Delta**).

Because we started from the MLE solution spreadsheet (Figure 4.3A) and the iterative procedure converged on an upper bound for β, to find a lower bound we next input a starting value for β lower than the MLE of 0.64302. We return to the spreadsheet shown in Figure 4.3A and change B2 to, say, 0.3. After that we proceed exactly as previously shown in Figures 4.5A through 4.9A. Remember to adjust the **Solver** input to change only cell A2. Once again, convergence is reached after three iterations, and the lower bound for β is 0.4333. The interval (0.4333, 0.9069) is an approximate 95% confidence interval for the shape parameter β. For bounds on α, repeat the iterations just described, reversing the roles of A2 and B2.

**NOT E:** If convergence is not achieved and/or likelihood values in column G cannot be calculated, try different starting values until you have convergence.

Weibull Distribution 121

#### **Problems**

4.1 A population of devices are known to fail according to a Weibull distribution with characteristic life  $\alpha$  = 200,000 hours. Evaluate the probability a new device will fail by 1,000, 4,000, 10,000, 40,000, and 100,000 hours for cases where the shape parameter is 0.5, 1.0, and 2.5. Calculate the failure rate (in FITs) at these times for the three shape parameters.

- 4.2 A radio manufacturer uses four different resistors as part of a tuner system. The resistor manufacturer specifies that each resistor has a lifetime modeled adequately by a Weibull distribution with shape parameter 2.0. The four resistors have characteristic lives, in hours of average radio usage, of 1000, 1200, 1500, and 2000 hours, respectively. What is the life distribution for time to first resistor failure? What is the radio MTTF? (Hint:  $\Gamma(\frac{3}{2}) = 0.88623$ .) What is the median failure time for the radio? How likely is it that no resistor fails in the first 168 hours? In the first 1000 hours?
- 4.3 An experiment to estimate Weibull parameters produced the following data: 10 exact times of failure at  $t_1, t_2, ..., t_{10}$ ; 5 more failures in the readout interval  $(0, T_1)$ ; and 7 more fails between  $T_1$  and  $T_2$ . The mixture of exact times and readout times came about because two test chambers were used, only one of which had continuous monitoring capability. The chamber with exact failure times ended test at time  $T_2$ , with 10 unfailed units. The other chamber also ended test at time  $T_2$ , with 8 unfailed units. Write the equation for LIK. How would LIK change if you learned that the failure at time  $t_7$  was caused by a chamber mishap, and not by the failure mechanism under investigation? (Hint: See the discussion in Chapter 2, Section 2.11, on failure mode separation.)
- 4.4 As a follow-up to Example 4.6, assume that the vendor supplying the 101 parts tells you that the burn-in fallout from the production that produced these parts was 20 components. In other words, 121 components were burned-in an equivalent time to 5000 field hours and Table 4.4 shows the field data for the 101 parts that survived the burn-in. Use this information to find Weibull MLEs for the population these parts were sampled from. Are these estimates similar to the estimates obtained in Section 4.2A?
- 4.5 The 10 exact failure times in Problem 4.3 are 134, 456, 700, 718, 819, 901, 912, 1234, 1689, and 1893 hours.  $T_1$  is 1000 hours and  $T_2$  is 2000 hours. Find MLEs for the Weibull parameters assuming the fail at 901 hours was real, and then find the MLEs if that fail was an experimental mishap. For each analysis, find 95% confidence intervals for  $\beta$  and  $\alpha$ .
- 4.6 Simulate data from a stress test on 100 units, assuming the failure times follow a Weibull distribution with  $\alpha = 10,000$  hours and  $\beta = 0.75$ . Do 100 iterations. For each iteration, estimate the characteristic life  $\alpha$ , using the time to the 63<sup>rd</sup> failure, and estimate the median or  $T_{50}$ . Using the estimated characteristic life and the median, estimate the shape parameter for each sample via the expression

$$\beta = \frac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln(T_{E0}/\alpha)}$$

Generate histograms from the 100 estimates for both  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$ . Comment on the results.

### <span id="page-159-0"></span>Normal and Lognormal Distributions

The lognormal distribution is a popular life distribution model for many high technology applications. In particular, it is very suitable for semiconductor degradation failure mechanisms. It has also been used successfully for modeling material fatigue failures and failures due to crack propagation. Some of its success comes from its theoretical properties; in other cases, it "works" because it is flexible and fairly easy to use.

The primary purpose of this chapter is to discuss the properties and areas of application of the lognormal distribution. Many of these properties come directly from the properties of the normal distribution because a simple logarithmic transformation changes lognormal data into normal data. Anything we know how to do with the normal distribution and normal data, we can therefore do for the lognormal distribution and lognormal data. For that reason, we start this chapter with a review of the normal distribution.

#### 5.1 Normal Distribution Basics

Figure 5.1 shows the familiar bell-shaped curve, that is, the normal probability density function (PDF). This curve is defined over the entire x-axis, from  $-\infty$  to  $+\infty$ . This domain of definition differs from the life distributions in the previous four chapters, which were defined only on the positive x-axis. The equation for the normal PDF is

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-x)^2/2\sigma^2}$$

with the two parameters designated by  $\mu$  (mu, the mean and a location parameter) and  $\sigma$  (sigma, the standard deviation and a scale parameter). As Figure 5.1 indicates, the distribution is symmetrical about its center  $\mu$  (located at 0 in Figure 5.1), and  $\sigma$  is a scale parameter that indicates how close to the center the area under the curve is packed. A range of  $\pm 1\sigma$  from the center contains about 68% of the area or population,  $\pm 2\sigma$  contains about 95%, and  $\pm 3\sigma$  covers 99.7% of any normal population.

The parameters  $\mu$  and  $\sigma$  are natural in the sense that  $\mu = E(X)$ , the mean, and  $\sigma^2 = E[(X-\mu)^2]$ , the variance for a normal random variable X. The standard deviation,  $\sigma$ , is the square root of the variance.

The cumulative distribution function (CDF) for the normal distribution is obtained by integrating the PDF and has an *S* shape as shown in Figure 5.2. The hazard function is defined for all real *x* but has limited value in a failure rate context, since the normal distribution is seldom used as a life distribution model.

**FIGURE 5.1** The normal distribution PDF.

**FIGURE 5.2** The normal distribution CDF*.*

If we start with a normal random variable *X* with parameters μ and σ, a simple transformation yields

$$Z = \frac{X - \sigma}{\sigma}$$

This transformation is known as standardization and *Z* has the "standard" normal distribution, which is a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The symbols  $\phi(z)$  and  $\Phi(z)$  are commonly used to represent the standard normal PDF and CDF, respectively. The respective equations are

$$\phi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}$$

and

$$\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{z} (z) dz$$

The CDF for the normal distribution cannot be expressed in closed form by integration of the PDF. Thus, tables obtained by numerical integration procedures or approximation formulas are used. Because any normal variable can easily be transformed into a standard normal by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, one set of tabled values for  $\Phi(z)$  has wide applicability. Since by symmetry  $\Phi(z) = 1 - \Phi(-z)$ , many authors provide values of the CDF only for positive z, that is, starting at  $\Phi(0) = 0.5$ . For ease of calculation, Table 5.1 gives values of  $\Phi(z)$  from z = -4.09 to z = 4.09, in steps of 0.01. This table will handle most applications. Alternatively, many handheld calculators and statistical software packages provide CDF values directly for many distributions, including the normal. The spreadsheet expression NORMSDIST(z) returns the standard normal CDF  $\Phi(z)$ , and NORMSINV(Area) returns the standard normal z value corresponding to a given area or CDF. We can also use the expression NORMDIST(x,  $\mu$ ,  $\sigma$ , 1) to get the CDF for a normal distribution with mean  $\mu$  and standard deviation  $\sigma$ , evaluated at x. Replacing "1" in the fourth argument with "0" evaluates the PDF at x. (For OpenOffice, use semicolons instead of commas between arguments.) JMP's formula editor includes the standard normal CDF (under Probability), and Minitab allows input of a mean and a standard deviation for evaluating the normal CDF in the Calc menu under Probability Distributions.

Any area under the normal PDF curve, or any probability or population proportion, can be calculated from Table 5.1. An example will illustrate the techniques involved.

#### **EXAMPLE 5.1 NORMAL DISTRIBUTION CALCULATIONS**

An electronics manufacturer uses interconnection wire which has a mean strength of  $11\,g$  (i.e., it takes an average pull force of  $11\,g$  to break the wire). If the population distribution about this average value is normal with a standard deviation of  $1.2\,g$ , find the following:

- The proportion of wires that will survive a pull of 13 g
- The probability a wire breaks under a load of 8 g
- The proportion of wires that will survive a pull of at least 8.5 g but not over 13.2 g

#### SOLUTION

Before we can use tables based on the standard normal distribution, we have to standardize the numbers given in the problem. The proportion greater than 13 for a normal distribution with  $\mu$  = 11 and  $\sigma$  = 1.2 is the same as the area to the right of (13 – 11)/1.2 = 1.67 for a standard normal distribution. This area is 1 –  $\Phi$ (1.67). Table 5.1 gives  $\Phi$ (1.67) = 0.95254, and so 1 – 0.95254 = 0.04746. We would get approximately the same answer with the spreadsheet expression 1 – NORMDIST(13, 11, 1.2, 1).

The probability a wire breaks under an 8 g load is just  $\Phi[(8-11)/1.2] = \Phi(-2.5)$ . We look up  $\Phi(-2.5)$  in Table 5.1 and obtain  $\Phi(-2.5) = 0.00621$ . Alternatively, we could type the spreadsheet function NORMSDIST(-2.5) and get the same result.

#### **EXERCISE 5.1**

A soft drink vending machine dispenses liquid into an 8 oz cup. The target value is 8.0 oz, and the cup will take up to 8.72 oz before overflowing. The lower limit before customer dissatisfaction is 7.5 oz. Assume the distribution of fill is normal with a mean that is on target at 8.0 oz and standard deviation of 0.25 oz. What is the probability of overflow? What is the probability a cup being filled below the lower limit? What is the amount of liquid corresponding to the 0.5% point of the fill distribution?

Some additional properties of normal random variables extend the usefulness of the standard normal CDF values given in Table 5.1 even further. These properties are as follows:

1. If X and Y are independent normal random variables with X having mean  $\mu_x$  and standard deviation  $\sigma_x$ , and Y having mean  $\mu_y$  and standard deviation  $\sigma_y$ , then the sum W = X + Y is also distributed normally with mean  $\mu_w = \mu_x + \mu_y$  and standard deviation

$$\sigma_w = \sqrt{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2}$$

This property can be extended to the sum of any number of independent normal variables by adding more mean terms to get the mean of the sum, and adding more variance terms under the square root sign to get the standard deviation of the sum. Independence means that  $P(X \le x \mid Y = y) = P(X \le x)$  or, in words, knowing the value of Y gives you no information about the value of X.

2. Linear combinations of independent normal random variables are also normal. For *X* and *Y* as in property 1, Z = aX + bY is normal with mean  $(a\mu_x + b\mu_y)$  and standard deviation

$$\sqrt{a^2 \,\sigma_x^2 + b^2 \sigma_y^2}$$

3. If  $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$  are a random sample of observations from a normal population with mean  $\mu$  and standard deviation  $\sigma$ , then the sample mean

$$\overline{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i / n$$

also has a normal distribution with mean  $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$  and standard deviation  $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$ .

#### **EXAMPLE 5.2 ROOT-MEAN-SQUARE EXAMPLE**

A computer designer must carefully control the delay time it takes signals to travel from one location within a system to another, so that they arrive at their destination on time according to the system "clock." Each component within a given path has a specified mean delay, as well as a 3-sigma upper and lower bound to use in testing the safety of the design. Assume a given path has four stages, two of which have mean delays of 10 ns, with a 3-sigma upper bound of 13 ns, and the other two have mean delays of 8 ns, with a 3-sigma upper bound of 11 ns. Characterize

the mean and 3-sigma upper bound of the total path and estimate the probability a delay is longer than 42.5ns.

#### **Solution**

The rules given for calculating the mean and standard deviation of a sum of independent normal random variables are valid even if the assumption of normality is dropped. The average or mean total path delay is the sum of all the mean delays (independence is not even required for this property to hold). Thus, the mean delay is 10 + 10 + 8 + 8 = 36. If the delays at each stage are *independent*, the value of sigma for the total delay is the square root of the sum of all the individual variances. 3-sigma for the first two stages is 13 − 10 = 3, and so sigma for each of these is 1. 3-sigma for the next two stages is 11 − 8 = 3, and again sigma is 1. The total path sigma is the square root of 12 + 12 +12 +12, or 4 2 = .

Since normality is usually a reasonable assumption for delay lengths, the probability of any delay exceeding 42.5 ns can be calculated by finding 1− Φ[(42. ) 5 3 − 6 2/ ] = 1− Φ(3.25) = 0.0006, from Table 5.1. Note that adding up 3-sigma limits for each stage (i. e., adding 13 + 13 + 11 + 11 = 48) would give an upper limit on the path delay equivalent to 6 sigma units (36 + 6 × 2 = 48). This (sometimes called "worst case design") limit would be unrealistic.

An electronic component acts to transform an input signal of level *X* into an output signal of level *Y* = 3*X* + 2. If *X* is normally distributed with mean 10 and standard deviation 2, estimate the average and standard deviation of *Y*. Find the probability that *Y* exceeds 40. #### **5.2 Applications of the Normal Distribution**

As the last example showed, the normal distribution is frequently used to model measurement errors of almost any kind. In addition, many of the populations frequently encountered in industrial (or other) applications generate sample results that give bell-shaped symmetrical histograms that can be fitted adequately by the normal PDF.

Even if a population has a skewed histogram, which cannot be modeled by a normal distribution, the mean of a sample from this population (or *x* ), considered as a random variable in its own right, will tend to have a more nearly normal shape. (This property is a consequence of the central limit theorem [CLT], described in Section 5.3.) Therefore, we can use the normal distribution to model populations of sample means, with nearly universal success. This feature may not seem very useful, but in fact, it is the basis for evaluating results from statistically designed experiments (DOE) and for the wide applicability of control chart techniques for monitoring industrial processes through statistical process control (SPC).

For any process we want to maintain at its best operating level, we can take regular samples of a key process parameter and treat the sample averages as if they were normally distributed. A control chart has upper and lower lines usually located 3-sigma units above and below the overall process parameter average. Note the sigma we speak of here is that of the sample averages, or σ/ *n*, where σ is the population standard deviation for the individual values and *n* is the number of measurements included in each average. Based on the properties of the normal distribution, only about three sample averages in a 130 *Applied Reliability*

thousand should fall outside of the region bounded by the 3-sigma lines. In other words, plus or minus 3-sigma limits from the center of the population contain 99.7% of the population values, as can be calculated from Table 5.1 by looking at the area to the left of three and to the right of minus three. So any point that does fall outside the control limits is highly unusual and unlikely, unless something abnormal happened to change the process. Control charts are discussed in more detail in Chapter 11.

If we investigate the process every time an "out-of-control point" outside of the control limits occurs, we will be chasing false alarms only an average of three times in a thousand, or once a year if we take one sample every day, 7 days per week. This rare false alarm is a small price to pay for an alert system that tells us when some unusual variability has probably been introduced into our process.

#### **EXERCISE 5.3**

A process has established a stable mean at 10.5 μm. The population standard deviation for the individual values is 0.5. If sampling consists of four measurements for each consecutive time period, calculate the 3-sigma upper and lower control limits for this process.

#### **5.3 Central Limit Theorem**

The CLT, which ensures the approximate normality of *x*, has many versions. Most statements involve intricate mathematical conditions. (See Gnedenko, Belyayev, and Solovyev 1969, page 33, for an example.) For our purposes, a heuristic verbal statement will suffice.

Under fairly general conditions, the CLT shows that the sum of a large number of random variables, each of which contributes only a small amount to the total, will have an approximately normal distribution. As the number of contributing factors increases, with the share of each growing smaller, the approximation becomes more exact.

The sample average, as the sample size *n* increases, is a perfect example of a situation satisfying the conditions of the CLT. Each term in the sum *x x* = + + ( /*n x* ) ( / ) *n x* + ( /*<sup>n</sup> n*) 1 2 grows smaller as *n* increases, and the distribution of *x* approaches normality *no matter what underlying distribution the xi come from* (as long as this distribution has a finite mean and variance). In terms of practical application, when *n* is as little as 4 or 5, *x* typically shows good normal characteristics.

Another excellent example is the variability introduced whenever anything is measured. Measurement errors generally (or usually) come from a multiplicity of small random factors, combining to produce a deviation from the "true" value of the quantity under measurement. Repeated measurements produce a histogram with a normal shape, as one would expect from the CLT. In fact, the great nineteenth-century mathematician Karl Gauss derived the normal distribution as the appropriate model for measurement errors, and it is often called the Gaussian error distribution.

An example similar to measurement error would be the variability when a mechanical operation is repeated over and over again. (This property formed the basis of Example 4.3, where we saw that normal errors in two coordinate directions led to a Rayleigh distribution for the radial error.) The rule of thumb of designing so that 3-sigma deviations from mean are within specifications comes from assuming that manufacturing variation and repeatability variation lead to a normal-shaped variability about the mean value, and plus or minus 3-sigma limits will therefore capture 99.7% of the population.

The CLT justifies the empirical observation that the normal model works for many types of data, since it makes sense to model many important random phenomena as the sum of a large number of small contributing factors. Since fitting a normal model to data means picking a  $\hat{\ }$  estimate of  $\mu$  and a  $\hat{\ }$  estimate of  $\sigma$ , methods of estimation will be looked at in the next section.

#### 5.4 Normal Distribution Parameter Estimation

For complete samples of observations from a normal distribution, the standard estimates for the mean and standard deviation are well known and the best that can be used. For a sample of size n, the estimates are

$$\hat{\sigma} = \overline{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i / n, \quad \hat{\sigma} = s = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(x_i - \overline{x})^2}{n - 1}}$$

These are also the MLEs (that is, maximum likelihood estimates), except that the MLE of  $\sigma$  has a divisor of n, instead of (n-1), which is a negligible difference for large sample sizes. The reason for using (n-1) instead of n is that it corrects for a slight bias inherent in the MLE.

If the data is censored or multicensored or grouped by readout intervals, the standard estimates no longer apply. Either graphical estimation (see Chapter 6) or computer programs using the maximum likelihood method can be used. This latter approach is treated extensively in Cohen and Whitten (1988); see also Bain and Engelhardt (1991), Nelson (1982), and Meeker and Escobar (1998). Minitab allows choice of the normal distribution in its **Reliability/Survival** platform and can be used to find MLEs for censored data. JMP does not include (as of release 7) the normal distribution as an option for censored data analysis, but data modifications, followed by a lognormal analysis, can be used, as is shown in Section 5.9. The same modifications can also be used with the spreadsheet template described in Section 5.9 to obtain normal distribution parameter estimates from multicensored data.

The graphical method is equivalent to the fitting of a straight line through the data points plotted on normal probability paper and using the slope of the line and the 50th percentile interception value to calculate  $\sigma$  and  $\mu$  estimates, respectively. The graphical approach starts by setting the CDF estimate at any of the data points, or readout times, approximately equal to the standard normal CDF  $\Phi$  evaluated at the appropriate normalized

point. The inverse of  $\Phi$  is then applied to derive an equation that is linear in the unknown parameters  $\mu$  and  $\sigma$ . The equations are

$$\Phi \frac{x-}{\sigma} = F(x)$$

$$\Phi^{-1}\Phi \frac{x-}{\sigma} = \Phi^{-1}F(x)$$

$$\frac{x-}{\sigma} = \Phi^{-1}F(x)$$

$$x = +\sigma \Phi^{-1}F(x)$$

The last equation is the key one, since it links an observable variable x to a quantity  $\Phi^{-1}F(x)$  that can be calculated from the CDF estimate corresponding to x. Indeed, this linear equation is the basis of normal probability plotting, discussed in Chapter 6.

For r exact observations, with n-r censored out of a sample of n, first order the points so that  $x_i$  is the ith smallest ( $x_1$  is the smallest), and then estimate the CDF  $F(x_i)$  using median ranks or approximately (i-0.3)/(n+0.4), as described in Chapter 6. However, if the data comes in grouped intervals with endpoints  $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k$ , then estimate  $F(x_i)$  by the number of observations less than or equal to  $x_i$ , divided by n. (The rationale for these CDF estimates is given in Chapter 6).

The quantity  $\Phi^{-1}(F)$  can be obtained, with a little work, from Table 5.1. For example, if F = 0.62, look up this value on the probability scale and find that the z value that has  $\Phi(z) = 0.62$  is approximately 0.31. Therefore,  $\Phi^{-1}(0.62) = 0.31$ . If we want  $\Phi^{-1}(0.33)$ , we look in Table 5.1 and obtain z = -0.44. This shows  $\Phi^{-1}(0.33) = -0.44$ . For more exact values, spreadsheets have the function NORMINV(x,  $\mu$ ,  $\sigma$ ). Alternatively, the function NORMSINV(F) provides the z value directly corresponding to a specific area under the standard normal curve. The JMP formula editor has **Normal Quantile (z)**, and Minitab has **Inverse Cumulative Probability** (select **Calc**, then **Probability Distributions**, then **Normal**).

This survey of some of the properties of the normal distribution has been included primarily for what will be needed when we discuss the lognormal life distribution. #### 5.5 Simulating Normal Random Variables

As described in Chapter 1, random variables may be simulated through the use of the uniform random variable defined in the interval (0,1) and inverse expressions for the desired CDFs. Specifically, if F is any CDF with an inverse  $F^{-1}$ , then substitution of the unit uniform random variable U for F in the inverse expression  $F^{-1}$  will generate a random variable distributed according to F. Thus, the spreadsheet formula NORMSINV(RAND()) will generate a pseudorandom standard normal variable, which can then be multiplied by  $\sigma$  and added to  $\mu$  to obtain a simulated variable from a normal distribution with mean  $\mu$  and standard deviation  $\sigma$ , denoted by  $N(\mu, \sigma)$ . JMP and Minitab have routines that will simulate random normal data.

#### EXAMPLE 5.4 SIMULATION OF $C_{PK}$ DISTRIBUTION

Let us consider a quality control example involving a stable process with measured values modeled by a normal distribution. Recall that 99.73% of normally distributed values are contained within  $\pm 3\sigma$  units, and so  $6\sigma$  is commonly used to represent the process width or spread. We are interested in how closely the center of the distribution comes to the nearest, either upper or lower, specification limit. We define the process capability index,  $C_{pk}$  (see Montgomery 2009), as the minimum of the distances of the process center to either specification limit divided by  $3\sigma$ , which is half the process spread. Thus,

$$C_{\rm pk} = \min\left(\frac{\rm USL - \mu}{3\sigma}, \frac{\mu - \rm LSL}{3\sigma}\right)$$

where USL and LSL represent the upper and lower specification limits, respectively, and  $\mu$  is the process mean. Since the process standard deviation is estimated by the sample standard deviation s, which will vary from sample to sample,  $C_{\rm pk}$  is a statistic whose value will also vary; that is,  $C_{\rm pk}$  will have its own sampling distribution. In the absence of applicable theory, simulation can provide distributional properties of  $C_{\rm pk}$  for specified conditions.

For this example, we will consider a one-sided  $C_{\rm pk}$  for a LSL. Let us assume that a quality control document states the following for a sampling scheme: Take a random sample of 30 units from a process lot and estimate  $C_{\rm pk}$ . If  $C_{\rm pk}$  so determined is less than 1.6, hold the product for disposition.

**TABLE 5.3** Results of Simulation Example (1000 Iterations per *C*pk)

| Incoming Lot Cpk            | 1.2 | 1.3 | 1.4 | 1.5 | 1.6 | 1.7 | 1.8 | 1.9 | 2.0 |
|-----------------------------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| Probability of Lot Hold (%) | 99  | 91  | 80  | 66  | 44  | 30  | 15  | 7   | 3   |

Otherwise, ship the product. What is the probability a lot is held, given the true value of *C*pk? In this case, simulation involves the generation of 30 pseudorandom variables from a normal population. With σ equal to 1 for simplicity, the mean for each simulation run is set so that its distance to the LSL, in units of sigma, achieves a desired population process capability index, *C*pk. For example, for a *C*pk target of 1.6, the mean must be 4.8 sigma units above the LSL. For each group of 30 simulated samples, corresponding to a lot with the preselected mean and σ, we estimate μ and σ and then *C*pk. For each possible *C*pk, the simulated lot sampling process is repeated for a sufficient number of iterations. A distribution of *C*pk values is thus produced to delineate the sampling distribution of *C*pk under the defined conditions.

We ran a simulation, using a spreadsheet program with random number generation capability, for *C*pk values from 1.2 to 2.0, in steps of 0.1. Based on 1000 iterations for each *C*pk value, the percentage of the number of *C*pk estimates that were less than 1.6 provided the basis for estimating the probability of lot hold. Table 5.3 displays the results.

We see that the incoming lot *C*pk must be considerably better than 1.6 in order to avoid lot holds. Further discussion of process capability indices can be found in Kane (1986) and Kotz and Johnson (1993).

#### **5.6 Lognormal Life Distribution**

The simple relationship between a normal random variable *X* and its derived lognormal random variable *tf* is the following: if *X* has mean μ and standard deviation σ, then *tf <sup>X</sup>* = e has a lognormal distribution with parameters *T*<sup>50</sup> = e and σ. Alternatively, if we start with a population of random failure times *tf* modeled by a lognormal distribution with median parameter *T*<sup>50</sup> and shape parameter σ, then the population of logarithmic failure times *X t* = *<sup>f</sup>* ln is normal with mean = ln*T*<sup>50</sup> and standard deviation σ (see Figure 5.4).

*The logarithm of a lognormal is normal*. In a mathematical sense, we never have to deal with the lognormal as a separate distribution; we can take logarithms (natural) of all the data points and analyze the transformed data as we would analyze normal data. This procedure is the basis for many lognormal analysis routines. After completing a normal analysis on the logarithmic time scale, the results are displayed in terms of the lognormal distribution and real time. The *T*<sup>50</sup> parameter of the lognormal distribution is a "natural" parameter in the sense that it is the median time to fail of the population of lognormal lifetimes. On the other hand, the parameter σ causes much confusion, as it is not a "natural" quantity describing the population of times to fail. σ should be thought of only as a shape parameter for the lognormal distribution. It is not the standard deviation of the population of lifetimes. But σ is a standard deviation, in units of logarithmic time, for the normal distribution describing the population of logarithmic times to failure. In a sense, σ is a

**FIGURE 5.4** Relationship of lognormal distribution to normal distribution.

"borrowed" parameter, only used for the lognormal distribution because of mathematical convenience.

#### 5.7 Properties of the Lognormal Distribution

The PDF for the lognormal distribution is given by

$$f(t) = \frac{1}{\sigma t \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(1/2\sigma^2)(\ln t - \ln T_{50})^2}$$

The CDF F(t) is the integral of the PDF from 0 to time t. It can also be expressed in terms of the standard normal CDF as

$$F(t) = \Phi\left\{\frac{\ln(t/T_{50})}{\sigma}\right\} = \Phi\left\{\frac{\ln t - \sigma}{\sigma}\right\}$$

This last equation allows us to use Table 5.1, or the spreadsheet function NORMSDIST, to evaluate probabilities of failure and survival for the lognormal distribution. We can also

use the spreadsheet expression LOGNORMDIST(t,  $\mu$ ,  $\sigma$ ) to evaluate the lognormal CDF at time t. Using Minitab, we go from **Calc** to **Probability Distributions** to **Lognormal** and then enter  $\mu$  for the *location* parameter and  $\sigma$  for the *scale* parameter. Then, we can calculate the lognormal PDF, CDF, or inverse function.

#### **EXAMPLE 5.5 LOGNORMAL PROPERTIES**

A population of components, when tested at high laboratory stresses, fail according to a lognormal distribution with  $T_{50}$  = 5000 and  $\sigma$  = 0.7. What percent of failures are expected on a 2000-hour test?

#### SOLUTION

Direct substitution gives

$$F(2000) = \Phi \frac{\ln(2000/5000)}{0.7} = \Phi(-1.309)$$

Using Table 5.1 or = NORMSDIST(-1.309), we get 0.095 or 9.5%.

The lognormal PDF has a wide variety of appearances, depending on the critical shape parameter  $\sigma$ . As shown in Figure 5.5, the variety of shapes lognormal data can have resembles the shapes taken on by the Weibull distribution (see Figure 4.2). This flexibility makes the lognormal an empirically useful model for right-skewed data. The similarity between Figure 5.5 and the Weibull PDF shapes shown in Figure 4.2 also suggests that both models

**FIGURE 5.5** The lognormal distribution PDF.

**FIGURE 5.6** The lognormal distribution CDF*.*

will often fit the same set of experimental data equally well. One trick that occasionally helps to choose whether a lognormal or a Weibull will work better for a given set of data is to look at a histogram of the logarithm of the data. If this is symmetrical and bell shaped, the lognormal will fit the original data well. If, on the other hand, the histogram now has a left-skewed appearance, a Weibull fit to the original data might work better.

Some examples of lognormal CDF curves are plotted in Figure 5.6. These curves show a long right-hand tail (right skew) for large values of σ. For a small σ such as 0.2, the PDF and CDF have a nearly normal shape.

The lognormal failure rate function *h*(*t*) has to be calculated using the basic definition *h*(*t*) = *f*(*t*)/[1−*F*(*t*)]. If the parameters are *T*<sup>50</sup> = e<sup>μ</sup> and σ, a spreadsheet expression for calculating the failure rate at time *t* is given by

NORMDIST(LN(
$$t$$
), ,  $\sigma$ , 0)/ $t$  \* (1 – NORMDIST(LN( $t$ ), ,  $\sigma$ , 1))

The various shapes that can be taken by the lognormal failure rate are shown in Figure 5.7. These are also similar to the variety of shapes taken on by the Weibull failure rate (as shown in Figure 4.4). Large values of σ behave like small values of β for the Weibull; if σ is larger than 2, the failure rate has a decreasing shape, although it always starts at 0 and rises to a maximum before decreasing. For large σ, the rise is so quick that, for practical purposes, the failure rate appears to decrease throughout life. Values of σ around 1 give failure rate functions that first rise quickly, then have a fairly constant failure rate for a long period of time. Low values of σ correspond to wear-out failure rates that are eventually rapidly increasing.

The mean time to fail (MTTF) for a lognormal distribution is given by

$$E(t_f) = \text{MTTF} = T_{50} e^{\sigma^2/2}$$

and the variance is

$$Var(t_f) = T_{50}^2 e^{\sigma^2} (e^{\sigma^2} - 1)$$

The true population standard deviation is, of course, the square root of the variance.

#### 5.8 Lognormal Distribution Areas of Application

The preceding section showed empirical justification for the suitability of the lognormal distribution as a life distribution model. The lognormal has a very flexible PDF and failure rate function, and its relationship to the normal distribution makes it convenient to work with.

Even though the lognormal and the Weibull models can fit most sets of life test data equally well, there is a major difference between the two that can have critical importance. This difference comes about when we use the fitted model to extrapolate beyond the range of the sample data.

If we have 100 units on test, the smallest percentile we can actually observe is the 1% point. We need a parametric model to project to the earlier time when 0.001% of the population might fail or to estimate a proportion of failures for a time much smaller than the time of the first observed test failure. If we use a lognormal model, the projection to smaller percentiles is usually optimistic, as compared to a projection based on a Weibull distribution fit. In other words, the lognormal will extrapolate lower average failure rates (AFRs) at early times. Sometimes the difference can be several orders of magnitude.

In Chapter 8, we will see that use-operating condition failure rates are often estimated from the very early percentiles of data obtained from a laboratory test conducted at high stress. How, then, can we decide whether it is appropriate to use the more optimistic lognormal model or the Weibull model?

A reasonable answer to this question is to look for a theoretical justification for one model or the other, based on the failure mechanism under investigation. In Chapter 4, we learned that the Weibull can be derived as the extreme value distribution that applies when many small defect sites compete with each other to be the one that causes the earliest time of failure. Similarly, there is a derivation that leads to the lognormal as a model for processes that degrade over time, eventually reaching a failure state.

The precise model that leads to a lognormal distribution is called a multiplicative (or proportional) growth model. At any instant of time, the process undergoes a random increase of degradation that is proportional to its present state. The multiplicative effect of all these random (and assumed independent) growths builds up to failure.

This model was used with great success by Kolmogorov (1941) to describe the dimensions of particles (such as grains of sand by the ocean) constantly undergoing a pulverizing process. References describing the multiplicative model include Mann, Schafer, and Singpurwalla (1974) and Gnedenko, Belyayev, and Solovyev (1969).

The derivation depends on viewing the process at many discrete points of time over the interval (0, t). Let  $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$  be random variables measuring the state of degradation of the process as we move along in time. The multiplicative model says that

$$x_i = (1+\delta_i)x_{i-1}$$

where  $\delta$  is the small proportional growth that takes the process from  $x_{i-1}$  to  $x_i$ . Then, it follows that

$$x_n = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 + \delta_i) x_0$$

$$\ln x_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln(1+\delta_i) + \ln x_0$$

$$\ln x_n \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i + \ln x_0$$

Now we invoke the CLT on the sum of the small random quantities  $\delta_i$ , and obtain that  $\ln x_n$  has an approximate normal distribution. Therefore,  $x_n$ , and hence  $x_t$ , has a lognormal distribution for any t. This argument shows that the probability the process has degraded to a failure state by time t is approximately given by the lognormal distribution.

This derivation gives us a theoretical reason to prefer a lognormal model when we can hypothesize a multiplicative degradation process is going on. Many semiconductor failure mechanisms could fit this model. Some examples are chemical reactions such as corrosion or material movement because of diffusion or migration or even crack growth propagation. It makes more sense to use a lognormal model for these kinds of failures than a Weibull (extreme value) model.

#### 5.9 Lognormal Parameter Estimation

If we have a complete sample of exact times to failure, then the best way to estimate  $T_{50}$  and  $\sigma$  is to take natural logarithms of all times of failure and then calculate  $\bar{x}$  and s for the sample of logarithmic data. The estimate of  $T_{50}$  is  $e^{\bar{x}}$ , and the estimate of  $\sigma$  is s. The formulas are as follows:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln t_i}{n}$$

$$S = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\ln t_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$$

$$\hat{T}_{50} = e^{\bar{x}}$$

If the data are censored or grouped by readout intervals, these estimates cannot be calculated with these formulas. Instead, we need a computer routine that calculates MLEs. In Examples 5.6 and 5.7, we will show how to use JMP and Minitab to solve for lognormal MLEs for censored and interval data. Appendix 5A shows how to use Excel.

Graphical methods can also be used to obtain (less precise) estimates. These procedures are described in Chapter 6. Here, we show a least squares technique for plotting

a straight line through the data points one would plot on lognormal probability paper. This method can be used for censored or readout data to estimate lognormal parameters. The estimates do not have the large sample optimality properties of MLEs, but when MLE computer routines are not available, this method is quick and reasonable to use.

The least squares technique is similar to that described in Section 5.4 for the normal distribution. By using the relationship between the lognormal and the normal, the linear equation involving the estimated sample CDF given in the section on normal parameter estimation becomes

$$\ln t_f = \ln T_{50} + \sigma \Phi^{-1} F(t)$$

Least squares estimates of  $\ln T_{50}$  and  $\sigma$  are obtained from any standard regression program by inputting the  $\ln t_i$  values as the dependent or Y variable, and the inverse normal transformation of the CDF estimates as the independent or X variable (similar to Example 5.3). After the least squares fit is completed, the slope estimate is  $\hat{\sigma}$  and the antilogarithm of the intercept is  $\hat{T}_{50}$ . See Chapter 6 for more detail on this approach.

# EXAMPLE 5.6 LOGNORMAL MLES AND LIKELIHOOD PROFILE CONFIDENCE LIMITS: EXACT TIMES OF FAILURE

A 4000-hour life test of 20 components yields 9 failures. Table 5.5 in Appendix 5.1A shows the exact times of failure data. Find the MLEs for  $T_{50}$  and  $\sigma$  for this data.

#### SOLUTION

The correct formats for either a JMP data table or a Minitab worksheet that will analyze Weibull exact failure time data are shown in Example 4.5. The format and analysis steps are no different for lognormal data, other than selecting that distribution as the assumed model. Figure 5.8 shows the Minitab inputs and output for this analysis. Remember, when using the Minitab Stat, Reliability/ Survival, Distribution Analysis (Right Censoring), Parametric Distribution Analysis platform, we need to select Lognormal for the Assumed Distribution, open the Censor window to enter the censor code column, and also open the Estimate window to choose maximum likelihood estimation (not the default in Minitab 15).

Note that Minitab gives a MLE of 8.334 for  $\mu = \ln T_{50}$  and calls this parameter the **location** parameter. The shape parameter  $\sigma$  is labeled the **scale** parameter, and the MLE is 0.578. The minimized negative log likelihood is shown as 85.370.

The JMP analysis inputs and output are shown in Figure 5.9. JMP calls the MLE for  $\mu = \ln T_{50}$  the **Intercept** term. The confidence bounds reported by Minitab (release 15) and JMP (release 7) differ slightly, since JMP uses the (preferred) profile-likelihood method for computing approximate confidence bounds, and Minitab uses a method based on the asymptotic normality of the MLEs.

Another difference in results between JMP and Minitab, for the analysis of exact times of failure data, has already been pointed out in Chapter 4 (Example 4.5). Releases of JMP prior to JMP 8 do not include a term in the negative log likelihood that equals the sum of the natural logarithms of the exact times of failure. This term has no effect on the MLE calculation, and JMP chooses to drop it in those earlier releases. However, Minitab includes it, as does the Excel template spreadsheet solution shown in Appendix 5A. #### 5.10 Some Useful Lognormal Equations

There are equations for the lognormal distribution that can facilitate estimation of parameters. We may be interested in solving for  $T_{50}$ , assuming  $\sigma$  and F(t) are known, or solving for  $\sigma$ , assuming  $T_{50}$  and F(t) are known, or even solving for t, assuming the other quantities are known. These alternatives are often useful, and the equations, along with spreadsheet equivalents, are

$$T_{50} = t e^{-\sigma \Phi^{-1}F(t)} = t * EXP(-\sigma * NORMSINV(F(t)))$$

$$\sigma = \frac{\ln(t/T_{50})}{\Phi^{-1}F(t)} = LN(t/T_{50})/NORMSINV(F(t))$$

$$t = T_{50}e^{\sigma \Phi^{-1}F(t)} = T_{50} * EXP(\sigma * NORMSINV(F(t)))$$

#### **EXAMPLE 5.8 LOGNORMAL CALCULATIONS**

What must the  $T_{50}$  of a lognormal distribution be in order to have 0.1% cumulative failures by 60,000 hours, assuming  $\sigma$  is known to be 0.8? What  $\sigma$  is needed in order to have an AFR over the first 40,000 hours of life of 0.05 %/K, given the  $T_{50}$  is 300,000? For this  $\sigma$ , how many hours does it take to reach 1% cumulative failures?

#### SOLUTION

We will use the normal Table 5.1. The reader can verify that the spreadsheet expressions lead to approximately the same results. We start with

$$T_{50} = 60,000 \,\mathrm{e}^{-0.8\Phi^{-1}(0.001)}$$

and from Table 5.1, we find  $\Phi^{-1}(0.001) = -3.09$ . Thus,  $T_{50} = 60,000e^{2.472} = 710,767$  hours.

To answer the second question, we first have to convert the AFR given to a CDF value. Note AFR(40,000) =  $10^5$  x {-ln R(40,000)}/40,000, where the factor of  $10^5$  is needed to convert the units to %/K. Setting this AFR equal to 0.05, we obtain R(40,000) = 0.9802 and F(40,000) = 0.0198. Using the formula  $\sigma = [\ln (40,000/300,000)]/\Phi^{-1}(0.0198)$  and the Table 5.1 value for  $\Phi^{-1}(0.0198) = -2.06$ , we obtain  $\sigma = 0.98$ . The time point when the CDF is 1% is given by

$$t = 300,000 e^{0.98\Phi^{-1}(0.01)} = 300,000 e^{0.98 \times 2.33} = 30,581$$

#### **5.11 Simulating Lognormal Random Variables**

We invoke the relationship of the lognormal distribution to the standard normal distribution to generate lognormal pseudorandom numbers. Thus, if *Z* has the standard normal distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1), then the random variable *T* defined by

$$T = e^{\sigma Z}$$

has a lognormal distribution with median μ and shape parameter σ. Thus, to obtain random lognormal values, we first generate the random, standardized normal values as discussed in Section 5.5, and then use the above expression for *T* to get the desired lognormally distributed random variables. Pseudorandom lognormal values can also be easily generated using spreadsheet functions. For example,

#### 1 E 00 \* ( XP 5 N\* ( ORMSDIST(RAND())

will simulate a pseudorandom value from a lognormal distribution with *T*<sup>50</sup> = 100 and σ = 5. Note: Using Minitab, it is possible to simulate data directly from a lognormal or many other distributions. Under the **Calc** menu, click **Random Data**, and select the desired distribution from the list. Enter the number of rows to generate and the parameters to fill a Minitab spreadsheet column with the random values from the distribution. JMP 7 or later also has the capability to directly simulate lognormal data.

#### **5.12 Summary**

The normal distribution, while not a suitable model for population lifetimes, finds many applications in reliability analysis because of its relationship to the lognormal distribution and its use as an error model and a model for control chart applications (see Chapter 9). Since any normal variable can be transformed into a standard normal variable by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, the standard normal table of CDF values given as Table 5.1 is frequently used. Alternatively, convenient spreadsheet functions are available.

Estimates of the normal distribution parameters μ and σ are *x* and *s* for complete samples. For censored and grouped data, graphical methods (Chapter 6), or the method of maximum likelihood, can be used. A simple regression procedure that objectively finds the best line to fit the data points to on normal probability paper can also be used to obtain estimates.

The lognormal distribution is a very useful and flexible model for reliability data. It is closely related to the normal distribution because the logarithm of a lognormal random variable has a normal distribution. The parameters of the lognormal distribution are its median, *T*50, and a shape parameter, σ. If we work in a logarithmic time scale, by taking natural logarithms of all the data points, the resulting normal population has mean parameter = e*<sup>T</sup>*<sup>50</sup> and standard deviation σ. This feature allows us to use normal distribution properties to calculate probabilities associated with a lognormal distribution.

The lognormal distribution can be derived from a model for degradation processes. The main requirement is that the change in the process at any time be a small random proportion of the accumulated degradation up to that time. This derivation may explain why the lognormal has been so successful modeling failures due to chemical reactions or molecular diffusion or migration. Some types of crack growth might also be expected to have a lognormal distribution.

Formulas and properties associated with the lognormal distribution are shown in Table 5.4. Estimation methods are identical to those mentioned for the normal distribution because of the close relationship between the lognormal and the normal. The best estimation method to use is maximum likelihood estimation, easily carried out for censored or interval data using JMP, Minitab, or the Excel template Genlnest.xls. You can also find profile-likelihood confidence limits for the lognormal parameters using JMP or Genlnest.xls.

# <span id="page-189-0"></span>Reliability Data Plotting

In the last three chapters, we discussed analytical techniques for estimating parameters for various distributions. However, it is also useful to have simple graphical procedures that allow checking the applicability of an assumed distribution model, quickly estimating parameters of that model, or displaying confidence regions of interest. The methods we show in this chapter permit rapid analysis of either exact times of failure data or readout data, that is, inspections or tests done at periodic intervals to check for new failures. Complete (all units fail) or single-censored data are treated. Multicensored data and arbitrary censoring (allowing for a combination of exact, left-, right-, and interval-censored data) are addressed in Chapter 7. We illustrate the procedures for the exponential, Weibull, normal, and lognormal distributions. We begin this chapter by first reviewing the properties of straight lines. Then, we describe the concepts of least squares (LS) regression analysis and linear rectification. This introductory material helps us understand the applicability of these methods to failure distributions.

#### 6.1 Properties of Straight Lines

Consider the straight line drawn through two points  $P_1$  at  $(x_1, y_1)$  and  $P_2$  at  $(x_2, y_2)$  in Figure 6.1. The *slope* of the line is defined as the ratio of the change in the y coordinates to the change in the x coordinates, for points on the line. Designating the slope by  $\beta_1$ , we have the following expression:

$$\beta_1 = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{y}{x}$$

Note the calculation of the slope is independent of the actual location of the points on the line, but the highest numerical precision will be obtained by selecting the two points as far apart as possible. We can write the above equation in the form  $y = \beta_1 x$ , which indicates that the change in y is proportional to the change in x, and the slope  $\beta_1$  is the proportionality factor. This property is called a linear relation.

Parallel lines have equal slopes. The significance of parallel lines in modeling accelerated stresses for several cells will be discussed in Chapter 8.

Consider the linear expression for any two points  $(x_1, y_1)$  and  $(x_2, y_2)$  on the line  $y_2 - y_1 = \beta_1(x_2 - x_1)$ . Fix the point  $(x_1, y_1)$ . For any (x, y) on the line,  $y - y_1 = \beta_1(x - x_1)$  or  $y = \beta_1 x + (y_1 - \beta_1 x_1)$ . Since  $y_1 - \beta_1 x_1$  is fixed, we can set this quantity equal to a constant  $\beta_0$  and write  $y = \beta_1 x + \beta_0$ .  $\beta_0$  is called the *intercept* because at x = 0, we get  $y = \beta_0$ , indicating that  $\beta_0$  is the y coordinate at the point where the straight line crosses the y-axis. An alternative expression for a straight line is

$$Ax + By + C = 0$$

where A, B, and C are constants. Any equation in this form (e.g., 3x - 4y + 2 = 0) describes a straight line.

**FIGURE 6.1** Straight line plot.

#### **EXERCISE 6.1**

Consider the two equivalent equations for a straight line:  $y = \beta_1 x + \beta_0$  and Ax + By + C = 0. Express  $\beta_1$  and  $\beta_0$  in terms of A, B, and C. Express A, B, and C in terms of B and B0.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.1 LINEAR EQUATIONS**

Let C and F denote, respectively, corresponding Celsius and Fahrenheit temperature readings in degrees. Given that there is a linear relation between the two readings, F and C, find the equation from the data: F = 32 at C = 0 and F = 212 at C = 100. Is there a temperature at which F = C?

#### SOLUTION

Use the linear relation

$$F_2 - F_1 = \beta_1(C_2 - C_1)$$

Then, the data shows

$$212 - 32 = \beta_1(100 - 0)$$

or

$$\beta_1 = \frac{180}{100} = \frac{9}{5}$$

At C = 0,  $F = \beta_0 = 32$ . So the equation is F = (9/5)C + 32. If we want the temperature at which F = C, we solve F = (9/5)F + 32 or F = -40.

When calculating electronic component reliability at use conditions, it is a common practice to select, often with little justification, 55°C as the ambient, operating system temperature. What is the Fahrenheit equivalent?

#### 6.2 Least Squares Fit (Regression Analysis)

Because of typical variation that occurs whenever measurements are made in experimentation, even if a linear relationship holds between two variables, observed data points can scatter around the expected line.

Is there a "best fit" line for a given set of data points? What do we mean by best fit? Assume *y* is the *dependent* variable and *x* is the *independent* variable. This designation means that in a given trial, we can set or choose a value for *x* and then observe the corresponding value for *y*. We would like to be able to accurately predict the *y* value from a given *x* value. Then, one definition of best fit would be to choose a line such that the sum of the squares of the deviations of the fitted, or predicted, *y* values from the actual observed *y* values is a minimum. In statistics, such a line is called an LS or *regression line* (see Figure 6.2).

It can be shown (Wackerly, Mendenhall, and Schaeffer 2008) that the equation of the best fitting (i.e., LS) line through *n* points is

$$\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_1 x + \hat{\beta}_0$$

where the true slope  $\beta_1$  of the regression line is estimated by the formula

$$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\overline{x} \cdot \overline{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\overline{x}^2}$$

**FIGURE 6.2** Regression line example.

The intercept estimate is  $\hat{\beta}_0 = \overline{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \overline{x}$ , where  $\overline{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i/n$ , the mean of x, and  $\overline{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i/n$ , the mean of y. Since  $\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_1 x + (\overline{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \overline{x})$ , when  $x = \overline{x}$ , we have  $y = \overline{y}$ , that is, the LS line always goes through the point  $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ .

In some cases, it is known that a functional relationship goes through the origin (0,0). For example, Ohm's law, V = IR, states that the voltage V across a resistor R is zero for zero current I. If we have a regression line through the origin (intercept is zero), the equation for the line is

$$\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_1 x$$

and the slope is estimated by

$$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}$$

One must be cautious about the general applicability of this reduced formula, since the statistical estimation properties are different from the formula containing an intercept term (see Kunter et al. 2005). We will highlight some important considerations in later examples.

Although the above formulas appear a bit tedious to evaluate, it is expected that individuals working in the field of reliability will have access to spreadsheet software or statistical packages that will perform the calculations. In particular, we will illustrate several different approaches using spreadsheet functions, JMP, and Minitab. Also, many inexpensive hand calculators are capable of LS regression calculations.

If certain assumptions (e.g., the deviations about the best fitting line are independent, normally distributed with expected value of zero, and have constant variance across all x values) are made concerning the linear model relating the dependent variable to the independent variable, then further statistical properties of the slope, intercept, and predicted values can be derived. The reader is referred to a text such as the one by Kunter et al. (2005) for a full discussion of this topic.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.2 REGRESSION LINE**

Find the regression line for the (*x*, *y*) pairs: (1, 3.1), (2, 4.0), (3, 5.1), (4, 5.7), and (5, 7.1).

#### SOLUTION BY MANUAL CALCULATIONS

Set up a simple table.

|      | х  | y    | $\chi^2$ | xy   |
|------|----|------|----------|------|
|      | 1  | 3.1  | 1        | 3.1  |
|      | 2  | 4.0  | 4        | 8.0  |
|      | 3  | 5.1  | 9        | 15.3 |
|      | 4  | 5.7  | 16       | 22.8 |
|      | 5  | 7.1  | 25       | 35.5 |
| Sums | 15 | 25.0 | 55       | 84.7 |

Then, 
$$\overline{x} = 3$$
,  $\overline{y} = 5$ ,  $n = 5$ ,  $\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{84.7 - 5 \times 3 \times 5}{55 - 5 \times 3^2} = 0.97$  and  $\hat{\beta}_0 = \overline{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \overline{x} = 2.09$ . Thus, the regression line is  $\hat{y} = 0.97x + 2.09$ .

The difference between the observed value, *y*, and the fitted value, *y*ˆ, that is, *y y* − ˆ, is called a *residual*. Plots of residuals are very useful for checking model assumptions. For example, residuals may be plotted against the predictor variable, *x*, the fitted value, *y*ˆ, or the time sequence of observations. Residuals may be checked for normality, constant variance, or any unusual patterns or trends. For further discussion, see Kunter et al. (2005).

#### **Solution via Spreadsheet Functions**

For data analysis, it is always a good idea to generate a scatter plot of *y* versus *x* using the graphical capabilities of the spreadsheet. Both Excel and OpenOffice have routines that automatically fit a regression line to the data. In Excel, after creating the graph, click once on the graphical points and then right click to show a menu. To add a fitted line to the graph, select **Add Trendline**. Under **Options,** choose to display the equation on the chart. Similarly, in OpenOffice, click the graphical points and then right click to show a menu. Select **Object Properties…, Statistics**, and **Linear Regression** under **Regression Curves.**

The primary spreadsheet functions are SLOPE and INTERCEPT. Arguments in Excel are separated by commas and in OpenOffice by semicolons. Opening a spreadsheet, we enter the *x* values in Example 6.2 into the column of cells A1:A5 and the *y* values into cells B1:B5. To estimate the slope and intercept, we can use the following: in Excel, SLOPE(B1:B5,A1:A5), which returns 0.97; in OpenOffice, INTERCEPT(B1:B5;A1:A5), which gives 2.09.

Note the SLOPE function cannot be used to force a line through the origin. To do so or to estimate certain statistical properties of the line, the alternative *array* function LINEST may be applied. Begin by highlighting two blank adjacent cells in a row for displaying the result and type LINEST(B1:B5,A1:A5) in Excel followed by pressing Ctrl+Shift+Enter simultaneously. Additional regression statistics are available in LINEST by highlighting a blank array of five rows and two columns and adding two binary (TRUE, FALSE or 1,0) arguments as in LINEST(B1:B5,A1:A5,1,1). If the third argument is 1 or TRUE, the intercept is calculated normally; if 0 or FALSE, the intercept is forced through the origin, that is, set to zero. If the last argument is TRUE, then the 5 × 2 output array includes the slope and intercept, the standard errors, the coefficient of determination (*r*2), the standard error of *y*, the *F*-statistic, and the degrees of freedom, along with the regression and residual sums of squares. The results are displayed in Table 6.1, in which we have also labeled the output in the respective adjacent array cells. For an explanation of these terms, refer to any applied text on regression methods, such as Kutner et al. (2005).

Another alternative is to use the statistical routines supplied as add-ins in spreadsheet software. For example, Excel makes available the add-in program **Analysis Toolpak**, which provides data analysis tools, including regression, which is accessible through the **Tools** menu (or **Data** menu in Excel 2007). The summary output displays regression statistics, analysis of variance, coefficients, residuals, confidence limits on the parameter estimates, and various graphs. For further information, consult the Excel Help menu or the texts by Middleton (2004) or Berk and Carey (2004).

#### **6.3 Rectification**

The techniques of linear regression can be used to estimate the constants and parameters of many equations, including some nonlinear forms, either directly or via a procedure called *linear rectification*. A simple example is the problem of determining a resistor's resistance value *R* from current and voltage pairs (*I,V*). The equation for Ohm's Law, *V* = *IR*, has the form *y x* = + β β 1 0 , with *y* = *V*, *x* = *I*, β<sup>1</sup> = *R*, and β<sup>0</sup> = 0. A plot of *V* versus *I* should approximate a straight line, going through the origin (0, 0), with slope *R*.

Next, consider the ideal gas law given by *PV* = *nRT*, where *P* is the pressure, *V* is the volume, *n* is the number of moles of gas present, *T* is the temperature, and *R* is the universal gas constant. Suppose we wish to determine *R* from an experiment in which the volume of 1 mole (*n* = 1) of gas is varied at a constant temperature (i.e., an adiabatic process) and the pressure is measured. A plot of *P* versus *V* would appear as shown in Figure 6.5.

**FIGURE 6.5** Ideal gas law plot.

**FIGURE 6.6** Ideal gas law plot using rectification.

If, however, *P* is plotted versus the reciprocal of *V*, that is *y* = *P* and *x* = 1/*V*, then for *P* = RT(1/*V)* or *y* = RT*x*, we should obtain a straight line with slope RT and zero intercept (*P* → 0 as *V* → ∞). Since *T* is fixed and known, *R* is simply determined. See Figure 6.6.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.3 LINEAR RECTIFICATION**

A model states the variable *Q* is proportional to some power of the variable *s*, that is, *Q sk* = α , where *k* is unknown and α is the unknown constant of proportionality. How do we determine *k* and α?

#### **Solution**

Taking logs of both sides of the equation, we get

$$\ln Q = \ln \alpha + k \ln s$$

If we now plot *Q* versus *s* on log–log scaled axes (or, equivalently, plot ln *Q* versus ln *s* on linear–linear axes) and the model applies, we should get a straight line with slope *k* and intercept α (or ln α on linear–linear axes). Note on log–log axes, the intercept is read directly at *s* = 1 because ln 1 = 0.

The concept of linear rectification (i.e., doing what is necessary to convert an equation into a linear form) is very important because it often allows us to estimate the parameters of a model easily from experimental data. For additional examples, see Baird (1995). This method of estimation will be used in Chapter 8. Now, however, we shall discuss the application of rectification to probability plotting of failure distributions.
