#### **6.4 Probability Plotting for the Exponential Distribution**

Probability plotting is a method for the graphical analysis of reliability data. The concept is simple: rectify the data in such a way that plotted points fall approximately on a straight line if an assumed distribution holds. If a straight line does not reasonably fit the data, other distributions may be tried. The failure distributions we discuss in this text can all be analyzed in this manner. We start with the exponential distribution. However, the procedures are general, and the later sections contain examples involving the Weibull, normal, and lognormal distributions.

There are two common approaches for obtaining reliability data from stress testing. A continuous monitoring system allows us to obtain exact failure times for stressed components while minimizing the possibility of handling induced failure modes unrelated to the actual stress. However, the data acquisition equipment required is generally quite costly.

A more common and less expensive method for reliability evaluation involves placing units under stress and inspecting them at fixed *readout* times. For example, a common readout schedule for integrated circuit stress testing (after an initial measurement at time zero) is 24, 48, 96, 168, 500, 750, and 1000 hours. At each readout, all units are taken off stress and tested to determine the numberfailing during the interval since the lastreadout. Then, good units are returned to stress, and failed units are typically forwarded to a laboratory for comprehensive failure analysis. The physical removal, test, and return of units to stress chambers involve some handling, possibly causing nonstress failures or disturbing potential failure mechanisms. For example, mobile ionic contamination on integrated circuits can lead to leakage failures, which can recover through baking if the applied stress voltage is removed while the oven temperature is still high. In readout situations, it is a good idea to use controls (unstressed units) that are tested along with the stressed units at each readout. At the final readout, the stressed units still surviving are considered singly (right) censored observations.

We illustrate probability plotting for the exponential distribution using both exact and readout data. These examples also show how the failure rate parameter,  $\lambda$  or the mean time to fail (MTTF), can be estimated via the slope of the straight line fit to the data.

#### 6.4.1 Rectifying the Exponential Distribution

Recall that the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the exponential distribution with MTTF and hazard rate  $\lambda = 1/MTTF$  is given by

$$F(t) = 1 - e^{-t/MTTF}$$

Rewriting this equation, taking natural logarithms, and solving for t, we get

$$t = \text{MTTF} \times \ln \frac{1}{1 - F(t)} = -\text{MTTF} \times \ln[1 - F(t)]$$

If the exponential distribution holds, plotting the time t on a linear y-axis against  $\ln \frac{1}{1 - F(t)}$  (or  $-\ln[1 - F(t)]$ ) on a linear x-axis should result in points that fall approxi-

mately on a straight line through the origin (zero intercept), with MTTF estimated by the slope of the line. Equivalently, one could plot t versus 1/[1 - F(t)] on linear–log (i.e., semilog) axes.

An alternative approach is to solve the above equation for the transformed CDF to get

$$-\ln[1 - F(t)] = \frac{t}{\text{MTTF}} = \lambda t$$

If the exponential distribution applies, plotting  $-\ln[1 - F(t)]$  on a linear *y*-axis versus the time *t* on a linear *x*-axis, or equivalently, 1/[1 - F(t)] versus *t* on log–linear axes should produce points that follow an approximate straight line going through the origin, with  $\lambda$  estimated by the slope.

Depending on which variable is considered the predictor and which is the dependent variable, the LS estimates of the distribution parameters MTTF or  $\lambda$  will differ. Practically, the differences will be minor. Since probability-plotting paper usually displays the transformed CDF on the vertical *y*-axis and the time (or log time) on the horizontal *x*-axis, probability plots created by commercial software programs typically follow that convention. Minitab fits the LS line by regressing time (or log time) versus the transformed CDF, that is, the time of failure is considered a response (dependent variable) for the transformed CDF as the fixed predictor (independent variable). JMP does not provide LS estimates as part of the survival

and reliability output, although LS estimates are possible via the model fitting section. Spreadsheet analysis allows one to choose either approach. For the examples that follow, we will create spreadsheet probability plots that treat time *t* or ln *t* as the dependent variable.

#### **6.4.2 Median Rank Estimates for Exact Failure Times**

We need to estimate the CDF *F*(*t*) associated with each time to failure. In Section 1.4, we estimated the CDF at a given time by dividing the cumulative number of failures *r* up to that time by the starting number of components *n*. An equal weight of 1/*n* is assigned to each failure. The estimate of *F*(*t*) is, thus, 1/*n* for the first-ordered failure time, 2/*n* for the second, and so on. In general, for the *r*th failure at time *tr*, we have

$$\hat{F}(t_r) = \frac{r}{n} \quad r = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n$$

This estimate for *F*(*t*), which holds for any failure distribution, is called *nonparametric* or *distribution free*, since no parametric failure distribution model is assumed. However, this method has an obvious problem. If we have only one unit on test and it fails at time *t*1, then *F t* ( )1 = 1. It is not realistic to expect that the one observed time to failure *t*<sup>1</sup> represents the 100th percentile of the population distribution. A median estimate *F t* ( )1 = 0 5. makes more sense for a single sample. Similarly, for the *n*th failure out of any *n*, this simple method assigns the unlikely value *F t*( ) *<sup>n</sup>* = = *n n*/ 1. We see that this estimate for complete failure data unreasonably implies that 100% of the population fails by the largest observed sample failure time *tn*.

Some authors (see the discussion in Hahn and Shapiro 1967) have suggested alternative estimators for *F*(*t*):

$$\widehat{F}(t_r) = \frac{r}{n+1}$$

or

$$\widehat{F}(t_r) = \frac{r - 1/2}{n}$$

Bernard and Bos-Levenbach (1953) show that these choices underestimate and overestimate, respectively, the slope of the true distribution line in more than half the cases.

Our choice, because of desirable statistical properties, is to use what are called "median ranks," especially since the values can be obtained conveniently from a built-in spreadsheet function. Median ranks were originally developed and applied in the article by Johnson (1951). To introduce the concept of median ranks, we start with some elementary aspects of *order statistics.*

Consider a random sample of *n* items that are stressed to failure and assume the population times to failure follow *any* lifetime distribution with CDF *F*(*t*). For example, suppose the recorded failure times (in hours) for a sample of five units, labeled A through E, are as follows:

| A  | B  | C  | D   | E   |
|----|----|----|-----|-----|
| 46 | 21 | 88 | 215 | 143 |

After arranging these times to failure by ascending magnitude, we obtain the corresponding *ordered* sample

| 21 | 46 | 88 | 143 | 215 |
|----|----|----|-----|-----|

The minimum is called the first-order statistic, denoted by  $T_{(1)}$ . The next higher value is the second-order statistic,  $T_{(2)}$ , and so on, up to the largest or nth order statistic,  $T_{(n)}$ , the maximum. In reliability experiments, ordered times to failure are naturally what we observe, since the failures occur sequentially in time. Each order statistic  $T_{(r)}$  is a random variable having its own CDF, with the CDF for the rth statistic denoted by  $F_{(r)}(t)$ . The population CDF F(t), evaluated at the median of  $T_{(r)}$ , which is the value of t where  $F_{(r)}(t) = 0.5$ , is called a t median t median rank is also the same as the median of the random variable t median rank at the t failure has the property that half the time it overestimates the true CDF at time t and half the time it underestimates the true CDF at the time t of t and property to have for an estimate of t and it turns out we can calculate these median rank positions independently of whatever distribution we are assuming for the CDF t.

In Appendix 6A, we present a more extensive treatment of median ranks. This theoretical discussion may be read later, if desired, to enhance understanding of median ranks. The calculation of the plotting positions given by these median ranks will be discussed next.

#### 6.4.3 Median Rank Plotting Positions

As discussed in Appendix 6A, median ranks apply to *any* distribution with arbitrary CDF F(t). Although tables are available (Johnson 1964), the median rank plotting position for the rth failure time in a sample of size n can be obtained directly from the inverse beta spreadsheet function BETAINV(0.5, r, n–r+1). For example, the median rank for the fifth failure in n = 20 units is given by BETAINV(0.5, 5, 16) = 0.22967.

If access to a spreadsheet is not available, we can use a simple, accurate approximation to median ranks from Bernard and Bos-Levenbach (1953), which is given by the formula

$$\hat{F}_{M_r}(t) \cong \frac{r - 0.3}{n + 0.4}$$
  $r = 1, 2, 3, ...$ 

To illustrate, the approximate median rank for the fifth failure in n = 20 is  $4.7/20.4 \approx 0.23$ . Because of desirable properties and simplicity, we recommend median rank probability plotting positions for any distribution.

It may seem appropriate that the regression line goes through the origin because the CDF generally takes on the value zero at time zero. However, there may exist what is called a *threshold parameter* or *guarantee time*, in which it is assumed that a unit cannot die before this threshold time. For example, fatigue failure may require time for crack initiation and propagation. This situation can be addressed with a two-parameter exponential distribution such as

$$F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda(t - \gamma)}$$

where  $\gamma$  is the threshold parameter. If there is physical justification for the existence of a nonzero threshold value, then forcing the line through the origin is not a good idea. In such cases, the fitted line is expected to intersect the time axis at approximately the value  $\gamma$  of the threshold parameter. For the distributions treated in this text, we shall assume zero for the threshold parameter. This topic is treated more extensively in Lawless (2003).

Note that there is an equivalence between the CDF and cumulative hazard function, since we have shown in Chapter 2 that

$$H(t) = -\ln[1 - F(t)]$$

An extensive treatment of an alternative approach based on cumulative hazard plotting is given by Nelson (1972). Properties of Nelson's method have been developed by Aalen (1978). However, the CDF procedure we have used is often preferred by reliability engineers, since the results follow from a simple transformation of the data. Unlike the CDF, the cumulative hazard has no simple interpretation other than its derivative equals the hazard rate, and so it becomes more difficult for an engineer to explain the analysis to others. Nevertheless, the cumulative hazard is a very useful mathematical concept, especially for handling multicensored data.

We plotted complete data (all units fail), but data censored at a single time (e.g., the test ends before all units fail) can similarly be plotted up to the last available exact time of failure. The analysis procedure is identical to that applied to complete data.

Ten units are stressed to failure. Exact failure times are measured at 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, 15, 30, 55, and 96 hours. Assuming an exponential model for the parent population, analyze the data using a probability plot based on median ranks. Estimate the MTTF.

We have used probability plotting to check the model validity and estimate parameters. However, the probability plot involved transformations of the CDF and also logarithmic

**FIGURE 6.9** Exponential model fit to data, exact times, LS MTTF estimate.

scaling. We recommend viewing the untransformed data distribution by plotting median rank CDF estimates versus the times to failure along with the model fit on linear–linear scales to understand how well the model fits the data. (Additionally, if desired, one can use nonlinear regression via the spreadsheet **Solver** routine to estimate the exponential parameter that minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals to further improve the nontransformed model fit.) Figure 6.9 shows the fit of the exponential model to the failure data with the previous LS MTTF estimate of 182.8 hours. Compare Figures 6.7–6.9 to gain further understanding of the effects of transformed axes.

#### **6.4.4 Confidence Limits Based on Rank Estimates**

With median ranks plotting positions, it is easy to provide confidence limits at the *r*th failure on either the CDF *F*(*tr* ) or the time *tr*. Johnson (1951) describes using rank estimates other than the median to determine confidence limits corresponding to the *r*th failure in a sample of size *n*. The spreadsheet function BETAINV for the inverse beta distribution makes this calculation straightforward. Simply enter the desired confidence level as the first argument of the spreadsheet function. The second and third arguments remain *r* and *n* − *r* + 1.

For example, suppose we want a 90% two-sided confidence interval for the population CDF at time *t5* associated with the 5th failure out of a random sample of *n* = 20 units. Using Excel, the upper limit is BETAINV(0.95, 5, 16) = 0.4010. The lower limit is BETAINV(0.05, 5, 16) = 0.1041. Thus, if we were to randomly select many samples of size 20 from the population, we would expect 90% of all the population CDF values *F(T(5*) ) associated with the fifth observation to be between 10.41% and 40.10%. We display 5% and 95% rank confidence limit estimates for the CDF at each failure time in Table 6.4. Figure 6.10 shows a spreadsheet-created probability plot with 90% confidence limits included. As shown, a 90% confidence interval is specific to the *r*th failure time. We may also calculate a 90% confidence interval at any other failure time. However, these pointwise intervals are not all simultaneously valid at 90% confidence. To determine a 90% confidence band for the entire curve requires different techniques that we will discuss in Section 6.7.

If the assumed distribution fits the data, we can use the estimated parameters obtained from the probability plot to convert the CDF confidence limits into bounds on the failure times (also referred to as quantiles or percentiles). These values are called confidence limits on the quantile function  $F^{-1}(p)$ , that is, the inverse value t corresponding to a specific CDF value where F(t) = p. Note, however, that while the bounds for  $F(T_{(r)})$  are exact and nonparametric, these bounds are approximate because of the need to estimate the MTTF and assume that the exponential distributional model is correct. To illustrate, assuming the exponential distribution and using the estimated MTTF  $\theta$ , we invert the exponential formula to get  $t = -\hat{\theta} \ln (1 - F)$ . We now use the upper and lower confidence limit estimates for F in the formula to get upper and lower confidence limits, respectively, for each  $t_{(i)}$ . For example, based on the previously estimated MTTF = 182.8 hours, the corresponding time for the 5th failure lower confidence limit is  $-182.8 \cdot \ln(1 - 0.104) = 20.09$  hours. The time for the upper confidence limit is  $-182.8 \cdot \ln(1 - 0.401) = 93.67$  hours. Thus, we are 90% confident that the true time to the 5th failure out of 20 units falls between 20.09 and 93.67 hours. We can do similar calculations for every rth failure as shown in Table 6.4. Then, these pointwise quantile limits can be associated with the median rank value for the rth failure to generate the graph shown in Figure 6.11. As opposed to the unevenly spaced confidence limits on the CDF associated with the random failure times, by plotting the model quantile limits at the transformed median rank positions we obtain a smoother appearing graph.

#### 6.4.5 Readout (Grouped) Data

For data from readout intervals, it is common to use the simple, nonparametric binomial estimate for the CDF, that is, the cumulative number of failures  $r_k$  at the kth readout divided by the starting sample size. Both Minitab and JMP use the binomial estimate for single right-censored interval data.

Let  $T_i$  be the (fixed) ith readout time, where i = 0, 1, 2, ..., m and  $T_0 = 0$ . Let  $d_i$  be the number of failures during the ith interval, that is,  $(T_{i-1}, T_i)$ , i = 1, 2, ..., m. This notation represents an open–closed interval, that is, we are considering times t such that  $T_{i-1} < t \le T_i$ . For readout data and starting sample size n, the CDF at the kth readout  $T_k$  is estimated by

$$\hat{F}(T_k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k d_i}{n} = \frac{r_k}{n}$$

As discussed previously for exact failure times, if all n units fail prior to any readout (complete data), the unrealistic implication of the binomial estimate is that the 100th percentile of the failure distribution is less than that readout time. Thus, for complete grouped data, it is a common practice to ignore the last data point for 100% failure, especially since in many cases such a value cannot be graphed in a probability plot.

We show in Table 6.5 readout times for a group of 100 components stressed in a study that ran to 600 hours. The data is singly censored because two components survived the final readout. The CDF is estimated at the end of each interval by the cumulative number of failures divided by n = 100. The spreadsheet probability plot is shown in Figure 6.12.

#### 6.4.6 Alternative Estimate of the Failure Rate and Mean Life

Note that at t = MTTF, the CDF has the value  $F(\text{MTTF}) = 1 - e^{-1} = 0.632...$  So an alternative estimator of the MTTF is the time where the plotted line intersects a vertical line located at F(t) = 0.632..., or equivalently where the transformed variable  $1/[1 - F(\text{MTTF})] = e \approx 2.7$ . Such a procedure is a quick way to get the MTTF for both exact and readout data without having to calculate the slope. It may be difficult to read off the MTTF value accurately using this procedure, but in many cases, it will suffice. Here, we estimate from the Figure 6.12 that the MTTF  $\approx 160$  hours or  $\lambda \approx 0.0063$  failures/h.

#### 6.4.7 Confidence Limits for Binomial Estimate for Readout Data

As described in Chapter 11, the maximum likelihood statistic for estimating the binomial proportion p is x/n, where x is the observed number of events and n is the sample size. The variance of p is given by

$$Var(p) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$$

When we use the binomial estimator for the CDF, where the event is a failure, the estimated standard error of *F* at time *t* is

$$\hat{s}(\hat{F}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{F}(1-\hat{F})}{n}}$$

Chapter 11 presents several approaches for estimating confidence limits for a binomial proportion. The normal approximation for  $100(1 - \alpha)\%$  confidence limits is given by

$$\hat{F} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \hat{s}(\hat{F})$$

where  $z_{1-\alpha/2}$  refers to the standard normal distribution  $100 \times (1 - \alpha/2)$  percentile. However, for large or small F, this method can result in values greater than 1 or less than zero. This approach is used in Minitab, with values outside of the interval (0,1) truncated at either 0 or 1. A logistic transformation is described in Meeker and Escobar (1998) that preserves the boundaries 0 and 1, and this procedure is used in **JMP**. A third approach is to apply the formulas for exact  $100(1 - \alpha)\%$  binomial confidence limits, as described in Chapter 11. This method is easily facilitated by the spreadsheet function BETAINV for the inverse beta distribution. Thus, at time t, for r observed cumulative failures in a sample of size n, the lower limit is 0 for r = 0 and BETAINV( $\alpha/2,r,n-r+1$ ) for r between 1 and n; the upper limit is 1 for r = n and BETAINV( $1-\alpha/2,r+1,n-r$ ) for r between 1 and n - 1. By using this procedure, we can estimate pointwise confidence limits for readout data. Based on the data in Table 6.5, we show the confidence limit calculations in Table 6.6 and the probability plot in Figure 6.13. Figure 6.14 is a CDF plot with approximate confidence limits on the time t (using the LS MTTF estimate of 158.76 hours).

The reader will note that the lower confidence limit for both exact times of failure (median rank plotting position) and readout data is calculated by BETAINV( $\alpha/2,r,n-r+1$ ). However, the upper limit for exact times of failure is given by BETAINV( $1-\alpha/2,r,n-r+1$ ), which differs from the readout data upper bound calculation of BETAINV( $1-\alpha/2,r+1,n-r$ ). Although one might think it strange that the upper bounds differ, it is more of a surprise that the lower bounds are the same. This is because the two situations are really quite different. When we have exact data, we observe the rth failure at a random time  $t_r$  and we are looking for bounds around the random quantity  $F(t_r)$ . When we have readout data, we know the time of the ith readout,  $T_i$ , and the number of failures, r, is random. So it is not surprising that the two different situations lead to different upper bounds.

#### **6.5 Probability Plotting for the Weibull Distribution**

The equation for the two-parameter Weibull distribution is

$$F(t) = 1 - e^{-(t/\alpha)^{\beta}}$$

where α, β, and *t* ≥ 0. As discussed in Chapter 4, we rewrite this equation in the form

$$1 - F(t) = e^{-(t/\alpha)^{\beta}}$$

and take natural logarithms of both sides twice and solve for ln *t* to get

$$\ln t = \frac{1}{\beta} \ln\{-\ln[1 - F(t)]\} + \ln \alpha$$

If the Weibull distribution holds, then a plot of ln *t* on a linear *y*-axis versus ln{ l − − n[1 *F t*( )]} on linear *x*-axis should result in points that approximately fall on a straight line with slope (1/β) and intercept ln α. Note that eintercept provides a simple and direct estimate for α, which does not depend on the β estimate. For graphical Weibull analysis on log–log scales, we can plot *t* versus −ln[1− *F t*( )], using the median ranks to estimate *F t*( ).

Alternatively, we may rewrite the last equation as

$$\ln\{-\ln[1-F(t)]\} = \beta \ln t - \beta \ln \alpha$$

If we rename the variables *y* = − ln{ ln[1 − *F*(*t*)]} and *x t* = ln , then (if the assumed Weibull model applies) a plot of estimated *y* values versus the corresponding *x* values should approximate a straight line with slope β and intercept −β lnα.

The LS parameter estimates for α and β will vary depending on which variable (*t* or the transformed CDF) is considered the predictor variable and which is the dependent variable. Minitab, for example, uses time or log of time as the dependent variable for LS estimates of the parameters. In most situations, the difference in estimates will be inconsequential.

Before the advent of software programs for Weibull analysis, special purpose Weibull graph paper was often used that permitted direct plotting of the estimated CDF versus time. These papers also had attached scales or nomographs that facilitated quick parameter estimation. We shall illustrate Weibull probability plotting using spreadsheets and then show how to use several different software programs for Weibull analysis on the same data.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.5 WEIBULL PROBABILITY PLOTTING: EXACT TIMES**

Twenty test devices are stressed to investigate dielectric breakdown strength. The test was concluded at 600 hours at which time 18 units had failed. The data is shown in Table 6.7. Estimate the parameters of the distribution from the graph: the shape factor  $\beta$  and characteristic life  $\alpha$ .

#### SOLUTION

For exact failures times, the estimation of F(t) is best done via median ranks, as shown in Table 6.7. The spreadsheet Weibull probability plot is shown in Figure 6.15. The straight line fit appears reasonable for the model.

The LS regression estimates obtained by regressing  $\ln t$  on  $\ln[-\ln(1-\hat{F}(t))]$  (using the spreadsheet SLOPE and INTERCEPT functions) are  $\alpha=82.924$  and  $\beta=0.5685$ . Note an alternative quick estimator of the characteristic life  $\alpha$  is found at the CDF value for which  $F(\alpha)=1-e^{-1}\approx.63$  and  $-\ln[1-F(\alpha)]=1.00$ . From Figure 6.15, we get  $\alpha\approx83$ .

**NOTE:** Lawless (2003) discusses properties of a three-parameter Weibull distribution, and Cran (1976) covers further graphical analysis.

We have used probability plotting to check the Weibull model validity and to estimate parameters. The probability plotting involves transformations on the CDF and logarithmic scaling. So again, it is advisable to look at the untransformed CDF estimates versus the failure times along with the Weibull model fit on linear scales to visualize how well the model fits. #### **6.5.2 Weibull Survival Analysis via JMP**

In a new data table, enter the times to failure and the censoring times into one column and the corresponding binary values, 0 for failure and 1 for censoring, in a second column. For exact times to failure, a frequency column is optional if each unit's failure or censoring time is individually listed. (Note for complete sample data, such as Exercise 6.8, all entries in the Censor column would be 0.) To see the graphs, choose **Analyze, Survival and Reliability, Survival/Reliability**. Complete the dialog box for **Y, Time to Event**, and **Censor**. Check **Plot Failure Instead of Survival**. Click **OK** and the output Failure Plot will appear. Click the small red icon in the title Product Limit Survival Fit to get a drop-down menu. Choose **Weibull Plot** and **Weibull Fit** to get output as shown in Figure 6.16. Note that the Product Limit Survival Plot will be explained in Chapter 7. The parameter estimates are MLE, since JMP does not directly provide LS estimates (LSE), although LS*E* can be easily obtained by using JMP's regression capabilities.

#### **6.5.3 Weibull Survival Analysis via Minitab**

Enter each individual failure and censoring time into one column called Time, or optionally, set up an additional column for frequency (Freq). Use of a frequency column simplifies data entry for multiple instances of the same failure or censoring times. Also as an option, into a third column for censoring (Censor), enter an F or 1 for each failure time and a C or 0 for each censoring time (reversing JMP's codes of 0 and 1 for the failure and censoring time, respectively). Select **Stat, Reliability/Survival, Distribution Analysis (Right Censoring), Parametric Distribution Analysis**. Select the **Time** column for variables and optionally the Freq column. Click **Censor…** For single censoring, select **Time Censor At**: and enter the censoring time. Optionally, click **Use Censoring Columns** and select the **Censor** column. Click **Estimate** and select **Maximum Likelihood**. Click **Graphs…** and check **Probability Plot, Cumulative Failure Plot**, and **Display Confidence Intervals**. Verify **Assumed Distribution: Weibull.** Graphs will appear as shown in Figure 6.17 along with tables of output.

The slight difference in parameter estimates in Minitab compared with the results reported previously for Example 6.5 is due to Minitab's use of approximate median rank estimates rather than those obtained from the BETAINV spreadsheet function.

#### **6.6 Probability Plotting for the Normal and Lognormal Distributions**

#### **6.6.1 Normal Distribution**

Let *X* be normally distributed and let *Z* be the standard normal variate, that is, *Z* = (*X* − μ)/σ, where (μ,σ2) are the population mean and variance. Recall that there is a one-to-one correspondence between *z* and the CDF, that is, the area to the left of *z* under the normal PDF curve. For example, *z* = 0 corresponds to a CDF value of 50%; *z* = −1.28 to about 10%; and so on. Thus, the CDF is uniquely associated with *z*. Following the notation in Chapter 5, designate this relation by the equation *z F* = Φ−1( ) with Φ−1( ) *F* denoting the inverse normal CDF function. We can rewrite the *z* equation as follows:

$$X = \sigma Z + = \sigma \Phi^{-1}(F) +$$

**FIGURE 6.16** JMP output Weibull model analysis, exact times.

FIGURE 6.17
Minitab output Weibull model analysis, exact times.

This last relation shows that if x is plotted on linear graph paper versus  $z = \Phi^{-1}(F)$  for the normal distribution, one will get a straight line with slope equal to the standard deviation  $\sigma$  and intercept (at F = 0.5 or z = 0) equal to the mean  $\mu$ . Consequently, if the normal distribution holds, sample data plotted against  $\hat{z} = \Phi^{-1}(\hat{F})$ , the inverse normal transformation of the estimated CDF, should approximate a straight line. The slope of the line estimates  $\sigma$ , and the intercept (50% point) estimates  $\mu$ , even for singly right-censored normal data.

For the normal distribution, the primary spreadsheet functions of interest are NORMSDIST and NORMSINV. The function NORMSDIST(z) returns the area under

the standard normal distribution corresponding to the standard normal variate z with mean 0 and variance 1. For example, NORMSDIST(−1.28) gives the value 0.100273, and NORMSDIST(1.645) results in 0.950015. Similarly, the function NORMSINV(CDF) returns the standard normal variate corresponding to the specified CDF. Thus, NORMSINV(0.01) gives the value −2.32635, and NORMSINV(0.8) results in 0.841621.

There are also the spreadsheet functions NORMDIST and NORMINV for normal distributions otherthan the standardnormaldistribution.Insteadof a single argument,these functions require several. For normally distributed *x* values, the forms are NORMDIST(*x*, mean, standard\_deviation, 0 or 1) and NORMINV(area, mean, standard\_deviation). For NORMDIST, the fourth argument of 1 or 0 determines respectively whether the output will be the cumulative area (CDF) under the normal curve to *x* or the height of the curve (PDF) at *x*. Thus, NORMDIST(1.25,1,0.5,1) gives 0.691462, and NORMDIST(1.25,1,0.5,0) results in 0.704131.

Prior to the development of software programs for reliability analysis, special purpose normal probability plotting papers were generally available. Now, however, one can plot a continuous factor *x* versus the *z* values obtained via spreadsheet functions on linear by linear axes. In either case, the slope and intercept can be estimated using the spreadsheet functions SLOPE and INTERCEPT.

We note that the normal distribution does not easily lend itself as a model for times to failure. Since the normal distribution spans negative infinity to positive infinity, and negative times to failure have no physical meaning, the normal distribution is not an ideal choice for a life distribution.

#### **EXERCISE 6.13**

100 units from a population of measurements believed to be normally distributed are randomly selected and measured. However, the measurement tool has a limited range, and consequently only the smallest 30 units can be measured. The smallest 30 values are ranked in order of increasing size and plotted on probability paper. The fit to a normal distribution appears reasonable and provides a standard deviation estimate of 5.0. Estimate the mean of the total sample (also an estimate of the population mean) given that the best fitting line on the probability plot goes through the CDF = 10% point at the value 72.9.

#### **6.6.2 Lognormal Distribution**

As discussed in Chapter 5, if the natural logarithms of failure times are normally distributed with mean μ and variance σ2, then the distribution of the times is lognormal with median *T*<sup>50</sup> = e and shape parameter σ. The median *T*<sup>50</sup> and the shape parameter σ are the standard parameters for expressing a lognormal distribution.

Similar to the normal, the rectifying equation is found by using the standard normal variate in the form

$$Z = \frac{\ln T - \ln T_{50}}{\sigma}$$

We rewrite this as

$$\ln t = \sigma z + \ln T_{50}$$

Thus, if the lognormal distribution applies, a plot of the natural logarithms of failure times versus *z F* ˆ = Φ−1( ), the inverse normal transformation of the estimated CDF, should approximate a straight line where the shape parameter σ estimate is the slope and the 50th percentile point is the estimate for *T*50.

Again, we have several plotting options. We can plot the following: (1) the z values obtained from a normal table or from the spreadsheet function NORMSINV( $\hat{F}$ ) versus the log of the failure times on linear–linear axes, (2)  $\hat{F}$  versus the log of the failure times on normal probability paper, or (3)  $\hat{F}$  versus the failure times on lognormal probability paper. All methods are basically equivalent, but computationally, a lognormal probability plot is the simplest.

For manual plots on lognormal probability paper, the slope can be estimated from the equation

$$\sigma = \frac{\ln \frac{t_2}{t_1}}{\Phi^{-1}[F(t_2)] - \Phi^{-1}[F(t_1)]}$$

or, since  $z = \Phi^{-1}(F) = 0$  at F = 50% and z = -1.00 at F = 15.9%,

$$\sigma = \ln \frac{T_{50}}{T_{15.9}}$$

As in the normal case, any convenient z multiple can also be used to estimate  $\sigma$ . Similarly, if  $T_{50}$  is outside of the range of the graph, the slope can be estimated and  $T_{50}$  solved from the equation

$$T_{50} = t e^{-\sigma \Phi^{-1}[F(t)]} = t e^{-\sigma z}$$

using any convenient time and percent failure combination. However, it is far simpler to use the spreadsheet functions SLOPE and INTERCEPT to estimate the lognormal distribution parameters.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.6 LOGNORMAL PROBABILITY PLOT**

600 transistors are tested under stress for 1000 hours. Each failure time is individually recorded. At the end of the experiment, 17 units have failed for a particular failure mode. The data are given in Table 6.8. It is assumed that the lognormal distribution applies. Check this assumption by plotting the data as a lognormal probability plot. Estimate the parameters of the distribution. How long a test do you expect is necessary to get 10% of the product to fail?

#### SOLUTION

The estimated CDF at each point using median ranks is shown in Table 6.8. The probability plot is shown in Figure 6.18. The LS regression line was determined by regressing  $\ln(t)$  on z using the spreadsheet functions  $\text{SLOPE}(\ln(t),z)$  and  $\text{INTERCEPT}(\ln(t),z)$ . The slope is 4.6445 and the intercept is 15.9244, and  $\text{e}^{15.9244}$  provides a  $T_{50}$  estimate of 8,238,973 hours. (Note: These values will differ slightly from the Minitab output, which is based on the approximate formula for median ranks.) The time to reach 10% failures is  $t = T_{50} \, \text{e}^{\sigma z_{0.10}} = 8.239 \times 10^6 \, \text{e}^{4.6445 \times -1.28} \approx 21,578$  hours. The CDF plot and lognormal model fit to the data along with rank estimate confidence limits are left as an exercise.

It is important to realize the amount of extrapolation involved in this example. We have observed less than 3% failures and are estimating a time to 50% failures at z = 0. As we can see from Figure 6.19, we are extrapolating nearly four orders of magnitude. Consequently, we can expect considerable variability in such estimates based on small percentages of observed failures.

#### **6.7 Simultaneous Confidence Bands**

We have previously discussed pointwise confidence limits, which apply at a specified time or quantile. However, there are situations in which we desire a *confidence band* for a distribution function *F*(*t*), that is, a set of upper and lower bounds that simultaneously capture the range of the assumed distribution with a chosen level of confidence. Note *F*(*t*) can be known or unknown. If *F*(*t*) is known, such a band could serve also as a goodness-of-fit

test of the assumed distribution for the sample data, since any estimated F(t) point falling outside the band would be evidence for rejection of the model.

Consider the following situation. The data consists of a complete random sample of failure times  $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n$  of size n from an unknown distribution function F(t). We would like a band that contains the unknown distribution F(t) completely within its bounds with 95% confidence.

This objective is possible by the application of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov D-statistic we have previously discussed in Chapter 3 relative to empirical distribution function (EDF) goodness of fit tests. Recall that the D-statistic measures the maximum deviation between the model distribution F(t) and the EDF  $F_n(t)$ . Based on a complete sample of size n, we can form a confidence band of width  $100(1-\alpha)\%$  by selecting a d-value from a table such that the probability of the D-statistic (designated  $D_n$ ) exceeding the d-value equals a specified  $\alpha$  risk, that is,

$$P(D_n \ge d) = \alpha$$

Hogg and Tanis (2001) show that the confidence band is defined then by

$$1 - \alpha = P[F_n(t) - d \le F(t) \le F_n(t) + d \text{ for all } t]$$

Note the band limits are bounded by 0 and 1, that is, the lower  $F_L(t) = F_n(t) - d \ge 0$  and the upper band limit  $F_U(t) = F_n(t) + d \le 1$ .

To determine d-value, we could reference a table of percentage points of the Kolmogorov statistics (see Miller 1956), available in many books on nonparametric statistics. However, as we discussed in the appendix to Chapter 3, by the application of a simple formula that incorporates the sample size n, D'Agostino and Stephens (1986) have provided a single line of significance points, for what they call the  $D^*$ -statistic. By inverting the formula, we can obtain the desired d-value. The formula for the d-value we use is

$$d = \frac{D^*}{\frac{\sqrt{n} + 0.12 + 0.11}{\sqrt{n}}}$$

where the  $D^*$  critical values for a two-sided significance level are shown in Table 6.9. We illustrate the usage of the table in Example 6.7.

#### 6.8 Summary

This chapter has reviewed graphical procedures that supplement the analytical tools covered in Chapters 1 through 5. We have discussed straight line concepts, LS regression, and linear rectification. We have shown how various distribution models can be checked for applicability using probability plots. In addition, we have demonstrated how quick parameter estimates can be obtained from the graphs and described several approaches for adding confidence limits. Special commercial probability papers can be used, or equivalent results may be obtained with linear or log papers coupled with simple transformations of CDF estimates. Spreadsheet programs, JMP, and Minitab also provide extensive graphical and analytical capabilities. These methods are easily applied to complete or singly right-censored data. We also covered the estimation of pointwise confidence limits for both the CDF and time to failure percentiles, along with a discussion of simultaneous confidence bands.

#### Appendix 6A

#### 6.1A Order Statistics and Median Ranks

Imagine a reliability study repeated a large number of times, with samples of size n from the same population with known CDF F(t). Since the time to the rth (ordered) failure will vary from sample to sample, there will be a distribution of times for the rth failure. Let  $F_{(r)}(t)$  denote the CDF of the rth-order statistic  $T_{(r)}$  in a sample of size n where  $r=1,2,3,\ldots,n$ . Consider the CDF  $F_{(n)}(t)$  of the largest order statistic  $T_{(n)}$ , that is, the maximum. By the definition of a CDF, we can write

$$F_{(n)}(t) = \Pr\left(T_{(n)} \le t\right)$$

For  $T_{(n)}$  to be less than or equal to t, it is necessary that all n times in the random sample be less than or equal to t. Since the CDF F(t) is the probability that the random variable T is less than or equal to t, assuming independence, we have

$$F_{(n)}(t) = [F(t)]^n$$

The median of the distribution  $F_{(n)}(t)$  is found by setting  $F_{(n)}(t) = 0.5$  in the above equation and solving for F(t) to get what is called the *median rank*  $F_{M_{(n)}}(t)$ , that is,

$$F_{M_{(n)}}(t)=0.5^{1/n}$$

For example, the median rank for the maximum in a sample of n = 5 is  $0.5^{1/n} = 0.87055$ . Similarly, for the smallest order statistic  $T_{(1)}$  with CDF  $F_{(1)}(t)$ , we see that

$$F_{(1)}(t) = \Pr\left(T_{(1)} \leq t\right) = 1 - \Pr\left(T_{(1)} > t\right)$$

For the smallest order statistic to be greater than t, it is necessary that all n times in the random sample be greater than t. Since 1 - F(t) is the probability that the random variable T is greater than t, we have

$$F_{(1)}(t) = 1 - [1 - F(t)]^n$$

The median of the distribution  $F_{(1)}(t)$  is found by setting  $F_{(1)}(t) = 0.5$  in the above equation and solving for F(t) to get the median rank,  $F_{M_{(1)}}(t)$ , that is,

$$F_{M_{(1)}}(t) = 1 - 0.5^{1/n}$$

For example, the median rank for the minimum in a sample of n = 5 is  $1 - 0.5^{1/n} = 0.12945$ .

We now consider the general result for  $F_{(r)}(t)$  following the approach by David and Nagaraja (2003). For the rth order statistic  $T_{(r)}$  to be less than t, at least r of the failure times  $T_i$  must be less than or equal to t. For example, in the random sample of five, the probability that the third-order statistic  $T_{(3)}$  is less than or equal to t includes the events that three, four, or five of the times  $T_i$  are less than or equal to t. Since the probability that  $T_i \le t$  is given by the CDF F(t), the probability that exactly t of the t are less than or equal to t is described by the binomial distribution (see Chapter 11). Consequently, the CDF t for the t th order statistic can be expressed as the sum of the individual binomial probabilities that exactly t of the t are t are t in the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t for the t

$$F_{(r)}(t) = \Pr(T_{(r)} \le t) = \sum_{i=r}^{n} \frac{n}{i} [F(t)]^{i} [1 - F(t)]^{n-i}$$

Note this result applies to *any* distribution with CDF F(t).

#### **EXERCISE 6.4A**

Using the results from the previous exercise, plot the CDFs of the second-, third-, and fourth-order statistics. Differentiate the CDFs to obtain the PDFs and create a graph of the PDFs.

We have specified above the CDF  $F_{(r)}(t)$  for any rth order statistic. Consequently, we should be able to find certain distributional properties such as the expected value or variance. Note that such parameters depend upon the specific form of the underlying distribution F(t). For example, if F(t) is uniform on [0,1], David and Nagaraja (2003) show that the expected value for the rth order statistic is r/(n+1). Some authors such as Plackett (1959) have used tabulated expected values of the rth order statistic, assuming F(t) is normally distributed, for plotting positions.

To avoid any distributional assumptions and also because the distribution  $F_{(r)}(t)$  may be non-symmetric or skewed, we focus on the median value of the distribution for the rth order statistic. Thus, we seek a general estimate for the population median CDF  $F_M(t)$  in the equation for the median of the rth order statistic:

$$F_{(r)}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i} [F_{M_r}(t)]^i [1 - F_{M_r}(t)]^{n-i} = 0.5$$

How do we solve for  $F_{M_r}(t)$ ? It can be shown (see Wackerly, Mendenhall, and Scheaffer 2008), that the cumulative binomial distribution is related to another probability distribution called the *incomplete beta function*. The relationship is

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i} [F(t)]^{i} [1 - F(t)]^{n-i} = I_{F(t)}(r, n-r+1)$$

where  $I_{F(t)}(r, n-r+1)$  is the cumulative distribution function for the beta distribution. Beta distribution tables are available (see Beyer 1968), but to solve easily for  $F_{M_r}(t)$  in the median equation, we can use the *inverse beta function* in a spreadsheet. The format for the median rank associated with the rth failure time is BETAINV(0.5,r,n-r+1), for n units on test.

To summarize, the population CDF F(t) evaluated at the median of the distribution of the times for the rth failure corresponds to the median rank plotting position. We show this property with the following example for an exponential distribution.

#### **EXAMPLE 6.1A ORDER STATISTICS FOR EXPONENTIAL DISTRIBUTION**

Five components randomly drawn from an exponential distribution with MTTF = 100 hours are stress tested. What is the median for the distribution of the first-order (minimum) statistic? What population CDF value corresponds to this median time? What is the median rank for the first-order statistic?

#### SOLUTION

The distribution of the first-order statistic, that is, the minimum, of a sample of five from an exponential distribution with  $\theta = 100$  hours is given by

$$F_{(1)}(t) = 1 - [1 - F(t)]^5 = 1 - [e^{-t/\theta}]^5 = 1 - e^{-t/20}$$

which is also exponential with MTTF<sub>(1)</sub> = 20 hours. To find the median for this distribution, we solve for  $t_{\text{med}}$  as shown:

$$F_{(1)}(t_{med}) = 1 - e^{-t_{med}/20} = 0.5$$

$$t_{med} = -20\ln(0.5) = 13.863$$

The population CDF F(t) at this median value is

$$F(t_{med}) = 1 - e^{-t_{med}/100} = 0.129449$$

To find the median rank for the first-order statistic, we use the spreadsheet inverse beta function BETAINV(0.5,1,5–1+1) that returns 0.129449, which is identical to the result found using the distribution of order statistics.

In addition to the median, the formula for CDF of the *r*th order statistic  $T_{(r)}$  can be solved for other confidence levels to obtain confidence limits. For example, for  $100(1 - \alpha)\%$  bounds, we can set

$$I_{F(t)}(r,n-r+1)=\frac{\alpha}{2}$$

190 Applied Reliability

and

$$I_{F(t)}(r, n-r+1) = \frac{1-\alpha}{2}$$

and solve using the BETAINV function. If the explicit form of the CDF  $F_{(r)}(t)$  allows for direct solution of the quantile t, then confidence limits are easily obtainable for both the CDF and time.

# EXAMPLE 6.2A CONFIDENCE LIMITS ON ORDER STATISTICS FOR EXPONENTIAL DISTRIBUTION

Five components randomly drawn from an exponential distribution with MTTF = 100 hours are stress tested. What is the 95% upper confidence limit for the distribution of the first-order (minimum) statistic? What is the 95% lower confidence limit for the distribution of the first-order (minimum) statistic? What population CDF value corresponds to the median first-order statistic time? What are the corresponding rank estimates for these limits?

#### SOLUTION

From Example 6.1A, the distribution of the minimum, of a sample of five from an exponential distribution with  $\theta = 100$  hours is exponential with MTTF<sub>(1)</sub> = 20 hours.

To find the upper 95% limit, we solve for  $\overline{t}$  as shown:

$$F_{(1)}(\overline{t}) = 1 - e^{-\overline{t}/20} = 0.95$$
  
 $\overline{t} = -20\ln(0.05) = 59.915$ 

The population CDF F(t) at this median value is

$$F(\overline{t}) = 1 - e^{-\overline{t}/100} = 0.45072$$

To find the 95% upper rank estimate for the first-order statistic, we use the spreadsheet inverse beta function BETAINV(0.95,1,5–1+1), which returns 0.45072, identical to the result found using the distribution of order statistics. To find the lower 95% limit, we solve for  $\underline{t}$  as shown below:

$$F_{(1)}(\underline{t}) = 1 - e^{-\frac{t}{20}} = 0.05$$
  
 $\underline{t} = -20\ln(0.95) = 1.02587$ 

The population CDF F(t) at this median value is

$$F(t) = 1 - e^{-\frac{t}{100}} = 0.010206$$

To find the 95% lower rank estimate for the first-order statistic, we use the spreadsheet inverse beta function BETAINV(0.05,1,5–1+1), which returns 0.010206, identical to the result found using the distribution of order statistics.

# <span id="page-229-0"></span>Analysis of Multicensored Data

In Chapter 6, we analyzed complete and singly right-censored data. We discussed estimating the cumulative distribution function (CDF) F(t) at time t by various methods, including median ranks for exact failure times and a binomial estimate for grouped data. These procedures did not invoke any specific distributional form. The CDF estimate was distribution free or *nonparametric*. The estimate F(t) could be tested for goodness of fit using probability plotting, chi-square, or various empirical distribution function (EDF) statistics to see if a specific parametric distribution model—such as the exponential, Weibull, or lognormal—was reasonable for the data. For exact failure times or grouped readout data with single right censoring, CDF estimation was fairly simple. However, there are many typical situations in reliability involving multiple censoring times, for both exact and disjoint interval data. Also, data may consist of combinations of exact failure times and left-, right-, or overlapping interval-censored observations, called arbitrarily censored data. We may experience what is called current status data, where only one inspection is made on each item for the presence or absence of a property (e.g., cracks in metal). Also, data may be left or right truncated. Nonparametric approaches to handle such analyses are the topics of this chapter. Pointwise and simultaneous confidence intervals are also discussed.

#### 7.1 Multicensored Data

The power of the methods described in this chapter lies in their ability to handle multicensored data (see Chapter 2), which is very common in reliability work and survival analysis. Situations under which multicensored data may arise are often unpredictable. For example, units under stress may fail for causes other than the expected mechanism. Environmental incidents such as electrical disturbances may destroy a portion of components under stress at a random time. Limited resources, such as oven space or receiving samples for stress on varying dates, may cause reliability tests to start on different times. During a stress, unfailed units may be removed periodically from test to track the progress of physical failure processes. Having the techniques to analyze such data is extremely valuable and can save reliability studies from becoming total losses because of unforeseen events.

#### 7.1.1 Kaplan-Meier Product Limit Estimation

The Kaplan–Meier (1958) product limit (PL) estimator is a long name for a very simple and useful procedure for calculating nonparametric survival probability estimates for incomplete data, consisting of exact failure and censoring times or data grouped into non-overlapping intervals. *Nonparametric* indicates that no failure distribution is assumed for analysis; that is, the methods apply to any lifetime distribution.

In the PL approach, the probability of components surviving any time interval is estimated by the ratio of the observed number of units surviving among the number of units at risk of

failure during the interval. Based on conditional probability concepts, the survival estimates for all successive intervals are multiplied together to provide a cumulative survival or overall reliability estimate at time *t*. The procedure is best illustrated by the following example.

#### **EXAMPLE 7.1 KAPLAN–MEIER PRODUCT LIMIT ESTIMATES FOR EXACT FAILURE TIME DATA**

A very common situation in medical or reliability studies occurs when objects under observation become censored for reasons (death, withdrawal, relocation, etc.) unrelated to the purpose of the study. For example, consider a stress designed to investigate open circuit failures caused by electromigration in a chip. Eight samples are placed on life stress and failures occur at 200, 250, 300, 400, 450, 500, 600, and 700 hours. Failure analysis subsequently determines that the failures at 250 and 450 hours are the result of an accidental electrical overstress that occurred only on these two units. These two failures, which were not caused by or related to electromigration, prevent us from obtaining complete electromigration failure data on all units. These two units provide survival information only up to their running times, which we call "censored times." Alternatively, we state that "losses" occur at 250 and 450 hours (see Figure 7.1).

At 200 hours, there is one failure out of eight units, and the simple probability estimate for a unit surviving 200 hours is 7/8 = .875. (Median rank considerations will be discussed later in this section.) A censored observation occurs at 250 hours, but because there are no electromigration failures between 200 and 300 hours, the survival probability estimate of .875 remains unchanged. When the second failure occurs at 300 hours, only six units are at risk of failure. For those six units, the probability estimate for surviving 300 hours, given that they have already survived 200 hours, is 5/6 = .833. The overall probability of surviving from time 0 to 300 hours, considering only failure times, is then estimated by the product of the sequential survival probabilities

$$P(T > 300) = (7/8)(5/6) = .729$$

In words, the probability of surviving 300 hours equals the probability of surviving 200 hours multiplied by the probability of surviving 300 hours *given* survival to 200 hours. In terms of conditional probability (see Section 1.5 on probability concepts in Chapter 1),

$$P(T > 300) = P(T > 200)P(T > 300|T > 200)$$

Just prior to the failure at 400 hours, there are five units at risk that have survived from 300 hours. Consequently, the conditional 400-hour survival probability is 4/5. The PL 400-hour survival estimate is

$$P(T > 400) = (7/8)(5/6)(4/5) = .583$$

**FIGURE 7.1** Eight units on stress: six failures and two censored (units 2 and 4).

At 450 hours, a second unit is censored. Thus, at the 500-hour failure, given survival to 400 hours, there are only three units at risk, and the 500-hour survival estimate is

$$P(T > 500) = (7/8)(5/6)(4/5)(2/3) = .389$$

The remaining survival estimates are similarly determined. The CDF *F*(*t*) at each failure time is estimated by subtracting the survival probabilities from 1. The estimated *PL* survival probabilities and CDF at all unique failure times are shown in Table 7.1. Step function plots of the survival curve and CDF are shown in Figure 7.2.

Let us now write the general expression for the Kaplan–Meier *PL* estimator (KMPLE). The notation may at first seem a bit daunting, but the final formula is easily understood. For example, if there are two units censored between the third failure at *t*<sup>3</sup> and the fourth failure at *t*<sup>4</sup> (*d*<sup>3</sup> = *d*<sup>4</sup> = 1), then *m*<sup>3</sup> = 2 with two censoring times *t*<sup>31</sup> and *t*32. Thus, the Kaplan–Meier *PL* estimate of the CDF *F*(*t*) is

$$\hat{F}(t) = 1 - \prod_{j=1}^{i} \frac{n_j - d_j}{n_i}$$

for i such that  $t_i$  " t. The product of individual terms is indicated by the multiplication symbol  $\prod_{i=1}^{n} X_i = X_1 X_2 \cdots X_i$ . This formula represents a step function at each failure time.

For example, using the data in Figure 7.1, we see that there are six failure times  $t_i$  where i = 1, 2, ..., 6 and  $t_{21}$ ,  $t_{31}$  are the two censoring times for the eight units. To estimate the CDF at, say, 325 hours, as  $t_2 = 300$  hours, we use

$$\hat{F}(325) = 1 - \frac{(8-1)}{8} \frac{(6-1)}{6} = 0.271$$

Thus, from the knowledge of the failure and censoring times, we can construct an estimate of the CDF for multicensored data. Then the estimated CDF can be tested for the applicability of any distributional form using the methods (e.g., probability plots) described in Chapter 6.

It is possible to estimate the variance of the CDF estimate  $\hat{F}(t)$  using a form of what is called Greenwood's formula (1926), expressed as

$$\widehat{Var}[\hat{F}(t)] = [1 - \hat{F}(t)]^2 \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{d_j}{n_j(n_j - d_j)}$$

for i such that  $t_i$  " t. For example, the variance estimate of the CDF estimate at 325 hours is

$$\widehat{Var}[\widehat{F}(325)] = (1 - 0.271)^2 \left[ \frac{1}{8(8-1)} + \frac{1}{6(6-1)} \right] = 0.0272$$

An estimate of the standard error of  $\hat{F}(t_i)$  is

$$\widehat{se}[\hat{F}(t_i)] = \sqrt{\widehat{Var}[\hat{F}(t_i)]}$$

The variance and standard error estimates of the CDF estimates for the failure times in Figure 7.1 are shown in Table 7.2.

Based on the CDF estimate  $\hat{F}(t)$  and standard error  $\widehat{se}[\hat{F}(t)]$ , we would like to establish pointwise confidence intervals on the population CDF. A normal linear approximation two-sided  $100(1-\alpha)\%$  confidence interval would be given by

$$[\tilde{F}(t), \tilde{F}(t)] = \hat{F}(t) \pm z_{(1-\alpha/2)} \widehat{se}[\hat{F}(t)]$$

**TABLE 7.2**Variance and Standard Error Estimates

| Time (hours) | CDF Estimate | Variance Estimate | Standard Error Estimate |
|--------------|--------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| 200          | 0.1250       | 0.01367           | 0.1169                  |
| 300          | 0.2708       | 0.02722           | 0.1650                  |
| 400          | 0.4167       | 0.03443           | 0.1856                  |
| 500          | 0.6111       | 0.04051           | 0.2013                  |
| 600          | 0.8056       | 0.02903           | 0.1704                  |
| 700          | 1.0000       | 0.00000           | 0.0000                  |

However, a CDF is restricted between 0 and 1, and the linear approximation for small sample sizes can result in a negative lower confidence limit  $\tilde{F}(t_i)$  or an upper confidence limit  $\tilde{F}(t_i)$  greater than 1. For example, at 325 hours, the linear approximation for a 95% confidence interval gives

$$[F(325), \tilde{F}(325)] = 0.271 \pm 1.96(0.165) = [-0.0525, 0.594]$$

At 650 hours, the similar linear approximation interval is [0.472, 1.140]. Clearly, these bounds are unreasonable for the population CDF. Some commercial software programs apply the normal linear approximation and simply truncate values below 0 or above 1.

Better approximations are possible by transforming the CDF estimate  $\hat{F}(t)$ , as first proposed by Borgan and Liestol (1990). The use of a transformation can create an unrestricted variable ranging between  $-\infty$  and  $+\infty$ , similar to a normal random variable. For example, we can apply the log transformation  $\ln[-\ln(1-F)]$ , which is actually a log transform of the cumulative hazard function  $H(t) = -\ln[1-F(t)]$  discussed in Chapter 2. Then we determine the standard error of the transformed function, possibly asymptotically, with a normal approximation. The actual derivation is beyond the scope of this text, but an example of this approach is provided in Kalbfleisch and Prentice (2002). Application of the normal approximation to the log transformation results in the approximate  $100(1-\alpha)\%$  nonsymmetric confidence interval given by

$$[\tilde{F}(t), \tilde{F}(t)] = [1 - (1 - \hat{F})^d, 1 - (1 - \hat{F})^{1/d}]$$

where  $d = \exp\left[\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{se}(\hat{F})}{(1-\hat{F})\ln(1-\hat{F})}\right]$ . For example, at 325 hours, a 95% approximate confidence

interval is found by first determining  $d = \exp\left[\frac{1.96*0.1650}{(1-0.2708)\ln(1-0.2708)}\right] = 0.2455$  and then evaluating

$$\{1 - [1 - \hat{F}(t)]^d, 1 - [1 - \hat{F}(t)]^{1/d}\} = [1 - 0.7292^{0.2455}, 1 - 0.7292^{1/0.2455}] = [0.0746, 0.7236]$$

Meeker and Escobar (1998) describe an alternative approximation that uses the more symmetric logit transformation logit( $\hat{F}$ ) = ln[ $\hat{F}/(1-\hat{F})$ ], leading to a slightly simpler form for the two-sided approximate  $100(1-\alpha)\%$  confidence interval

$$[\tilde{\xi}(t_i), \, \tilde{F}(t_i)] = \left[ \frac{\hat{F}}{\hat{F} + (1 - \hat{F}) \times w}, \, \frac{\hat{F}}{\hat{F} + (1 - \hat{F})/w} \right]$$

where  $w = \exp\{z_{(1-\alpha/2)}\widehat{se}(\hat{F})/[\hat{F}(1-\hat{F})]\}$ . Again, because  $\log \operatorname{it}(F)$  can vary between  $-\infty$  and  $\infty$ ,  $\log \operatorname{it}(F)$  is also unrestricted, similar to a normal random variable. These two methods assure that the confidence interval endpoints will always lie between 0 and 1. For example, for a 95% confidence interval at 325 hours, the logit transformation with

$$w = \exp\{1.96(0.165)/[0.271(1-0.271)]\} = 5.142$$

gives

$$\begin{split} [\tilde{F}(t_i),\,\tilde{F}(t_i)] = & \left[ \frac{0.271}{0.271 + (1 - 0.271) \times 5.142}, \frac{0.271}{0.271 + (1 - 0.271)/5.142} \right] \\ = & \left[ 0.0674,\,0.656 \right] \end{split}$$

The results for all failure times are shown in Table 7.3 and graphed in Figure 7.3.

In general, both the log-transformed and logit-transformed confidence intervals perform better than the normal approximation confidence interval, especially for small sample sizes. Both provide about the correct coverage probability of 95%, even with significant censoring. The log transform intervals are more conservative (e.g., wider) and less symmetric for smaller CDF values than the logit-based intervals. For very large samples, the three methods provide similar results.

One further point concerning the PL estimator for exact data can be made. Because the product limit estimate (PLE) reduces under no censoring, to the simple *i/n* plotting positions which we previously stated were not optimal, the estimator can be modified to produce approximate median rank estimators under multiple censoring. $$\hat{F}(t) = 1 - \frac{n + 0.7}{n + 0.4} \prod_{j=1}^{i} \frac{n_j - d_j + 0.7}{n_j + 0.7}$$

This modified expression improves the probability plotting positions when multiple censoring is involved.

#### **7.2 Analysis of Interval (Readout) Data**

Obtaining exact times of failures and losses is not always possible. As we discussed in Chapter 2, often reliability data comes from periodic readouts, generating interval data. Let us consider a different data collection scenario for the results shown in Figure 7.1, consisting of six failures and two losses. Instead of measuring exact times of failures or losses, assume we perform five consecutive weekly readouts, that is, at 168, 336, 504, 672, and 804 hours. The results are summarized in Table 7.6.

We are interested in estimating the survival probability at the end of each week. If we estimate the proportion entering each weekly interval that survive throughout the interval, then the end survival probability is estimated by the product of the estimated proportions for all prior intervals. However, the failures and censored observations occur randomly within each interval, and for the readout data, we are not certain when the losses occur relative to the failures. Consequently, the order of losses or failures within an interval is unknown.

| Summary of | f Readout (Inte | rval) Data     |                |
|------------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|
| Start Time | End-Time        | No of Failures | No of Censored |
| 0          | 168             | 0              | 0              |
| 168        | 336             | 2              | 1              |
| 336        | 504             | 2              | 1              |
| 504        | 672             | 1              | 0              |
| 672        | 840             | 1              | 0              |
|            |                 |                |                |

**TABLE 7.6**Summary of Readout (Interval) Data

Consider the interval 168 to 336 hours with two failures and one loss. Eight surviving units entered the interval. Did the loss occur before, after, or between the two failures? The different survival probabilities for the interval would be (5/7), (6/8), or (7/8)(5/6), respectively. In such cases where the specific time sequence is indeterminate, several alternative approaches are possible.

Let  $n_i$  be the number of items entering the ith interval,  $d_i$  the number of failures during the interval, and  $r_i$  the number of losses during the interval. If we assume all failures happen before any losses, the estimator for the ith interval is

$$\ddot{p}_i = \frac{n_i - d_i}{n_i}$$

If we assume all losses precede failures, the estimator is

$$p_i = \frac{n_i - d_i - r_i}{n_i - r_i}$$

Another intermediate value is obtained from the well-known "adjusted-observed" or "actuarial" estimate used in life tables:

$$p_i^{(a)} = \frac{n_i - d_i - r_i/2}{n_i - r_i/2}$$

This estimate is equivalent to assuming that half the censored observations within an interval precede and half follow the failures in that interval. For the second interval, the adjusted estimate is

$$p_{(a)}^2 = \frac{8 - 2 - 1/2}{8 - 1/2} = \frac{5.5}{7.5} = 0.7333...$$

Additionally, there is a "joint risk" (Kaplan and Meier 1958) estimate  $p_i$  for the ith interval given by

$$p_i = \frac{n_i - d_i - r_i}{n_i}^{\frac{d_i}{d_i + r_i}}$$

This estimate is the maximum likelihood estimate when the losses are random, the instantaneous rate for losses is a constant multiple of the rate for deaths, and the only data given are the values  $n_i$ ,  $d_i$ , and  $r_i$ . For the second interval, the joint risk estimate for the proportion surviving is

$$p_2 = \frac{8 - 2 - 1}{8}^{\frac{2}{2 + 1}} = 0.7310$$

We see that there is little practical difference between the actuarial and joint risk estimates. Using the latter estimate, the general expression for the Kaplan–Meier PL estimator for the CDF F(t) for interval data in which losses occur randomly during an interval is given by

$$\hat{F}(t) = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{k} \frac{n_i - d_i - r_i}{n_i}^{\frac{d_i}{d_i + r_i}}$$

Table 7.7 illustrates the joint risk and PL estimates under the assumption of random losses for the interval data. Note  $p_i = 1$  for an interval with no deaths or losses. As discussed in Section 7.1, confidence intervals using Greenwood's formula can be applied to these PLEs.

#### 7.2.1 Interval (Readout) Data Analysis in JMP and Minitab

Let us now see how JMP and Minitab treat interval (readout) data with multiple censoring. Data entry for both programs is similar. Each interval has a *start* time and an *end* time. Right-censored observations are entered with a start time and a missing value (blank cell in JMP or an asterisk symbol "\*" in Minitab) for the end time. Left-censored observations are entered with a missing value for the start time and the end time.

For random censoring within an interval, there are several options available in Minitab or JMP. Neither has the joint risk estimation capability, but Minitab has an actuarial estimate and JMP can provide an approximate actuarial estimate by some manipulation of the data. In future versions, it is expected that JMP and Minitab will have the capability to enter random censoring of failures and censored observations occurring within the same interval, such as the data in Table 7.6. Currently in both JMP and Minitab, one is required to treat censoring as occurring either at the beginning or end of an interval. However, random censoring can be approximated in most cases by performing two calculations, one with censoring at the beginning of an interval and the second with censoring at the end of the interval, and then averaging the resulting survival probabilities for each interval. We will illustrate these approaches in the examples in Sections 7.2.2 and 7.2.3.

#### **7.3 Life Table Data**

Because multicensored interval data naturally occur in the analysis of human mortality rates, we will briefly discuss actuarial life tables, which represent the oldest form of estimating the survival function. Life tables are a form of interval data involving specified time periods, in contrast to the *PL* estimator, which has failure or survival probabilities estimated at the observed failure time points. The actuarial method groups survival times into time periods, resulting in some loss of precision. The PL estimate makes use of the known survival times.

A life table shows the probabilities of a member of a particular population surviving (or dying) at a specific age. The specific periods of time are generally expressed in terms of equal intervals (years, weeks, months, etc.). In medical studies, it is a common practice to periodically add new groups (called cohorts) from the population of interest as a study progresses. Thus, for example, in the first year, there may be *n*<sup>1</sup> individuals with selected properties (e.g., having a certain disease) included. In the second year, *n*<sup>2</sup> patients might be added for the second cohort, and so on. Thus, at the end of five years, the study will have cohorts under observation for five years, others for four years, and so on. Consequently, the data is multicensored because at the end of the study the cohorts will have different censoring times. Additionally, some individuals in each cohort may be lost to the study for various reasons including death from other causes, moving away from the area, and so on. These losses must be factored into the analysis. Using the *actuarial estimate*, we will illustrate the procedure for the construction of a life table for multicensored data using an engineering example.

#### **EXAMPLE 7.2 ACTUARIAL LIFE TABLE ESTIMATION**

A company is concerned about the reliability of a new product received from a supplier. Typically 300 to 500 units are delivered each week for assembly into systems. Although the product was previously qualified, recent failures in prototype systems have been observed. A decision on following through with the planned shipment of this product in two months must be made. The reliability engineer decides that he will take a random sample of 10, 15, or 20 of the units received each week and placed them on a reliability stress. The units will be examined (readout) for failure at the end of each week. Six weeks will be allowed for the study. Occasionally, at random times a unit under stress will be removed from a group for physical failure analysis. At the end of 6 weeks, he will have some units on stress for 6 weeks, some for 5 weeks, and so on. Thus, the data is multicensored. The results of the reliability study are shown in Table 7.10. A notation commonly used in life tables is shown as the heading for the columns.

We see from Table 7.10, using the first sample for illustration, that 15 units were placed on stress and followed for 6 weeks. In the first week, one unit failed and one unit was removed for failure analysis. Consequently, entering the second week were 13 units alive on stress. No units failed the second week. One unit failed during the third week, four during the fourth week, none in the fifth, and one in the sixth. Seven units survived the 6 weeks of stress. The other five samples are similarly viewed. We now construct a life table using a spreadsheet based on these results.

We aggregate the data to create the columns shown in Table 7.11. The rows for the *lx*, *dx*, *ux*, and *wx* columns are the sums of the corresponding row entries in the matching columns in Table 7.10. The actuarial estimate is the basis for the column labeled "Effective Number of Units on Stress." In typical life tables, the individuals randomly removed during an interval are assumed to have been exposed to risk for only half the interval. Thus, the effective number of units on stress during the interval *x* to *x* + 1 would be estimated using the formula

$$I_x = I_x - \frac{u_x}{2}$$

In medical studies, if the patients enter the study randomly during the year, then the effective number would include a similar adjustment on the survivors  $w_x$  in a given time period, that is,  $I_x = I_x - (u_x + w_x)/2$ . In our example, we know that the units in each sample entered the stress together at the start of each week.

The estimated probability of failing during the interval x to x + 1, denoted by  $q_x$  is found by dividing the number of failures  $d_x$  by the effective number of units  $I_x$ . The probability  $p_x$  of surviving is  $1 - q_x$ . The cumulative probability of surviving from entry (time zero) through week x + 1 is denoted by S(x + 1) and is estimated by the product

$$S(x + 1) = p_0 p_1 p_2 \cdots p_x = \prod_{i=0}^{x} p_i$$

Note, for  $x \ge 1$ , that  $S(x + 1) = S(x)p_{x}$ , so the cumulative survival probability column is formed by successive multiplications of the values in the  $p_x$  column, with  $S(1) = p_0$ . The final column is created using the formula F(x + 1) = 1 - S(x + 1).

#### **7.4 Left-Truncated and Right-Censored Data**

Consider the following situation: We are interested in determining the life distribution after entering the field of a population of components that receive a 24-hour use conditions burn-in before shipment. We receive a sample of 100 post burn-in units to put on a 1000 hour stress. However, the number of components that failed during burn-in to produce these 100 units is not provided. The stress test is run, and at the end of 1000 hours, 20 units have failed and 80 still survive.

Here we have an example of data that is left-truncated and single right-censored. The CDF estimate at stress time *<sup>t</sup>* is for <sup>a</sup> population known to have survived <sup>24</sup> hours, that is, <sup>ˆ</sup> *F t*( ) at stress time *t* = 0 starts at the value zero and is a conditional CDF estimate for the population that has already survived 24 hours of normal operation. This is truncated data because we know nothing about the population prior to 24 hours of use. If we knew how many failures had occurred to get the 100 survivors, it would be left-censored data. Note that data similar to this was analyzed in Chapter 4 using maximum likelihood estimation methods (see Example 4.6) for the Weibull distribution. Here we consider nonparametric estimates for the CDF.

There are other situations in which left-truncated and multiple right-censored data can arise. An example is the Channing House data reported by Hyde (1980). This data gives the ages of death of elderly residents of a retirement community. The data is left truncated because only individuals beyond a certain age were allowed to enter the community. An unknown number of those who died prior to this age were excluded from the analysis. For each person joining the community, we have an age of entry and either the age of death or the censoring time. The analysis is based on the number of individuals actually present and at risk of death, when a death at a given age occurs. For small sample sizes, the CDF estimates may be highly variable. In such cases, it is best to start the CDF estimator at an age that yields a sufficient sample size and consider only death times beyond this age. The Kaplan–Meier PLEs have the remarkable property that they estimate the conditional CDF for units surviving to whatever age we start with, despite any earlier or later entries into the population (or multitruncated data). See Klein and Moeschberger (2003) for an analysis of the Channing House data.

For reliability engineering work, an analogy might be the analysis of data in which only those units that have seen a minimum age in the field are studied over some period of time. For example, a component manufacturer might be interested in the second-year survival curve for units having at least 1 year in operation. An unknown number of units less than 1 year of age may have already experienced the failure event of interest, leading to left-truncated data. Some items may fail during the second year and others may have no failures in the second year, resulting in right-censored observations.

The analysis of left-truncated and right-censored data can be easily accomplished in a spreadsheet by setting up one ordered column for the age of entry, death, or censoring, and a second coding column telling what the event recorded was. One then creates a third column of units at risk by adding one for each entry and subtracting one for each death or censoring event. Follow this by using the Kaplan–Meier *PL* estimation techniques (beginning at a specified age that has a reasonable sample size). Unfortunately, there is no way to enter data into Minitab or JMP and perform such conditional survival analysis.

#### **EXAMPLE 7.3 LEFT-TRUNCATED DATA**

A manufacturer sells a flashlight with a battery that is guaranteed for continuous operation for a maximum of 60 days. To start operating the light, the user removes an insulation strip between the battery and the circuit contact. After 60 days, the light output may decrease to an unsatisfactory level. An output 50% below the original is considered a failure. The manufacturer is interested in the reliability of the light for use beyond 60 days. The manufacturer has 20 units available for analysis, which are returned from the field with various ages of operation, nearly all beyond 60 days. The plan is to run these 20 units for an additional 60 days and determine the failure distribution. The results of the additional 60-days run on these 20 units are tabulated in Table 7.12. Estimate the cumulative failure probability based on the data.
